# Filesystem MCP Server

Node.js server implementing Model Context Protocol (MCP) for filesystem operations.

Published on npm as [`@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem).

## Features

- Read/write files
- Create/list/delete directories
- Move files/directories
- Search files
- Get file metadata
- Directory access control from command-line arguments, with [Roots](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/client-concepts#roots) as a deprecated, 2025-era convenience
- Serves both protocol eras on stdio: 2026-07-28 clients (`server/discover`, no handshake) and 2025-era clients (`initialize`)

## Directory Access Control

The server may touch only its **allowed directories**. Pass them on the command line. A 2025-era client that supports [Roots](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/client-concepts#roots) can also replace them at runtime, but Roots is [deprecated as of protocol version 2026-07-28](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/deprecated) and a 2026-07-28 connection cannot use it.

### Method 1: Command-line Arguments (Recommended)

Specify Allowed directories when starting the server:

```bash
mcp-server-filesystem /path/to/dir1 /path/to/dir2
```

Options may come before, between or after the directories: `--read-only`, `--read-only-dir <path>` (both below) and `--confine-roots` (under Method 2).

This is the only method that works on every protocol version, so it is the one to use.

### Read-only Mode

Add `--read-only` to serve only the tools that cannot change the filesystem:

```bash
mcp-server-filesystem --read-only /path/to/dir1 /path/to/dir2
```

The server then registers only the tools annotated `readOnlyHint: true` in the [Tool annotations](#tool-annotations-mcp-hints) table, the ones that read and list. Every tool not annotated `readOnlyHint: true`, that is every tool that writes (such as `write_file` and `edit_file`), is left out, so a client never lists it and a call to it fails as an unknown tool. A tool added later follows the same rule through its annotation. The server enforces this, whatever the client is configured to allow, and it works the same with `npx` as with Docker. It applies on both protocol eras, and to directories that come from a client's Roots.

The flag may appear anywhere among the arguments. `--` ends the options, so a directory literally named `--read-only` can be given after it.

Read-only mode covers every allowed directory. To make only some of them read-only, use `--read-only-dir` below.

#### Read-only directories

Add `--read-only-dir <path>` to make one directory read-only while the others stay writable. Repeat it for each directory to protect:

```bash
mcp-server-filesystem --read-only-dir /path/to/reference /path/to/workspace
```

- A read-only directory is an allowed directory too, so it need not also be listed on its own.
- Every write tool (`write_file`, `append_file`, `edit_file`, `create_directory`, `move_file` and `copy_file`) stays listed, since the other directories are writable, but refuses a target inside a read-only directory with an error such as `Access denied - read-only directory: /path/to/reference/notes.md is in /path/to/reference, which the server was started with --read-only-dir`. `move_file` is refused when either its source or its destination is inside one or contains one, so a protected directory cannot be carried away by moving its parent; `copy_file` may copy out of one, never into it. `edit_file` is refused there even with `dryRun`.
- The check runs on a path's resolved location, so a symlink in a writable directory cannot route a write into a read-only one. A read-only directory must therefore exist when the server starts: one that cannot be resolved (missing, not a directory, or a dangling symlink) stops the server from starting, rather than leaving a path it could not pin down writable.
- A path inside any read-only directory is refused, so a directory nested inside a read-only one is read-only too, even if it is also given as a writable directory.
- The marking is fixed at startup and holds on both protocol eras. A 2025-era client's Roots can replace the allowed directories (see Method 2), but Roots say nothing about writing, so they never lift it: a write into a read-only directory is refused whichever directories are in force, with or without `--confine-roots`.
- `list_allowed_directories` lists the read-only directories after the allowed ones, and the server logs them to stderr at startup.

The option may appear anywhere among the arguments, and takes the next argument as its directory, whatever it is. `--` ends the options, so after it `--read-only-dir` is a directory name. With `--read-only` as well, every write tool is withheld anyway. For defence in depth, make the protected directories read-only at the operating-system level as well, with file permissions or, with Docker, a bind mount's `ro` flag.

### Method 2: MCP Roots (Deprecated, 2025-era clients only)

A client that connects with a 2025-era protocol version (the `initialize` handshake) and supports [Roots](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/client-concepts#roots) can dynamically update the Allowed directories.

Roots notified by Client to Server, completely replace any server-side Allowed directories when provided.

#### Confining Roots to the command-line directories

To keep a client's Roots inside the directories you gave on the command line, add `--confine-roots`:

```bash
mcp-server-filesystem --confine-roots /path/to/dir1 /path/to/dir2
```

The client's Roots can then narrow the command-line directories but never replace or widen them. The server allows the overlap of the two:

- A root inside a command-line directory is allowed as given, so a client can narrow access to one project.
- A root that contains a command-line directory (for example `/`) is narrowed to that directory.
- A root outside every command-line directory is ignored

# mcp-server-git: A git MCP server

## Overview

A Model Context Protocol server for Git repository interaction and automation. This server provides tools to read, search, and manipulate Git repositories via Large Language Models.

Source: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/git

Requires MCP Python SDK 2.x (`mcp>=2.3,<3`). The server is built on the SDK's high-level `MCPServer`: each tool is a typed Python function, and the SDK derives its input schema from the signature.

Please note that mcp-server-git is currently in early development. The functionality and available tools are subject to change and expansion as we continue to develop and improve the server.

### Tools

1. `git_status`
   - Shows the working tree status
   - Input:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
   - Returns: Current status of working directory as text output

2. `git_diff_unstaged`
   - Shows changes in working directory not yet staged
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `context_lines` (number, optional): Number of context lines to show (default: 3)
   - Returns: Diff output of unstaged changes

3. `git_diff_staged`
   - Shows changes that are staged for commit
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `context_lines` (number, optional): Number of context lines to show (default: 3)
   - Returns: Diff output of staged changes

4. `git_diff`
   - Shows differences between branches or commits, or across a revision range
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `target` (string): Target branch or commit to compare with, or a revision range: `a..b` (from `a` to `b`) or `a...b` (from the merge base of `a` and `b` to `b`). An omitted endpoint means `HEAD`; each endpoint must resolve and cannot start with `-`
     - `context_lines` (number, optional): Number of context lines to show (default: 3)
   - Returns: Diff output comparing the working tree with target, or the two endpoints of a range with each other

5. `git_commit`
   - Records changes to the repository
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `message` (string): Commit message
   - Returns: Confirmation with new commit hash; an error if nothing is staged (as `git commit` without `--allow-empty`), except while a merge is in progress (`MERGE_HEAD` present), where git also allows an empty commit. While a merge is in progress the commit concludes it: its parents are `HEAD` and every `MERGE_HEAD` commit, and the merge state is cleared

6. `git_add`
   - Adds file contents to the staging area
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `files` (string[]): Non-empty array of file paths to stage; `["."]` stages everything
   - Returns: Confirmation of staged files, or a message saying nothing was staged when the call left the index unchanged

7. `git_reset`
   - Unstages all staged changes
   - Input:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
   - Returns: Confirmation of reset operation

8. `git_log`
   - Shows the commit logs with optional date filtering
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `max_count` (number, optional): Maximum number of commits to show, at least 1 (default: 10)
     - `start_timestamp` (string, optional): Start timestamp for filtering commits. Accepts ISO 8601 format (e.g., '2024-01-15T14:30:25'), relative dates (e.g., '2 weeks ago', 'yesterday'), or absolute dates (e.g., '2024-01-15', 'Jan 15 2024')
     - `end_timestamp` (string, optional): End timestamp for filtering commits. Accepts ISO 8601 format (e.g., '2024-01-15T14:30:25'), relative dates (e.g., '2 weeks ago', 'yesterday'), or absolute dates (e.g., '2024-01-15', 'Jan 15 2024')
   - Returns: Array of commit entries with hash, author, date, and message

9. `git_create_branch`
   - Creates a new branch
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `branch_name` (string): Name of the new branch
     - `base_branch` (string, optional): Branch, tag or commit SHA to create from (defaults to the current branch, or to the current commit when HEAD is detached)
   - Returns: Confirmation of branch creation, naming the base branch, or the short SHA when the base is a commit
10. `git_checkout`
   - Switches branches
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `branch_name` (string): Name of branch to checkout
   - Returns: Confirmation of branch switch, or `HEAD is now detached at <short sha>` when `branch_name` is not a branch (a sha, tag or other revision)
11. `git_merge`
   - Merges a branch into the current branch, or changes nothing
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `source_branch` (string): Branch, tag or commit to merge into the current branch (check out the branch to merge into first with `git_checkout`)
     - `fast_forward_only` (boolean, optional): Only fast-forward, failing if the branches have diverged (default `true`). `false` lets Git create a merge commit when they have
   - Returns: `Fast-forwarded`, `Merged ... with merge commit <short sha>`, or `Already up to date`
   - Refuses a detached HEAD, a working tree with uncommitted changes, a merge already in progress, and a merge that would overwrite an ignored local file. A merge that stops on conflicts is aborted (`git merge --abort`) and the error names the conflicting files, so the repository is left as it was
12. `git_show`
   - Shows the contents of a commit, or of a file or directory at a revision
   - Inputs:
     - `repo_path` (string): Path to Git repository
     - `revision` (string): The revision (commit hash, branch name, tag) or object spec (`HEAD:path/to/file`) to show
   - Returns: Contents of the specified commit, file content, or directory listing

     - `repo_path` (string): Path to the Git repository.

readme.markdown:
# Fetch MCP Server

A Model Context Protocol server that provides web content fetching capabilities. This server enables LLMs to retrieve and process content from web pages, converting HTML to markdown for easier consumption.

Source: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/fetch

Requires MCP Python SDK 2.x (`mcp>=2.3,<3`).

> [!CAUTION]
> This server can access local/internal IP addresses and may represent a security risk. Exercise caution when using this MCP server to ensure this does not expose any sensitive data.
>
> By default the server refuses to fetch private, loopback, link-local and other non-public addresses, including cloud metadata endpoints such as `169.254.169.254`, and checks every redirect hop the same way. The `--allow-private-ips` argument turns this guard off; see [Customization - Private addresses](#customization---private-addresses). The guard checks the addresses a hostname resolves to before each request, so it does not protect against DNS rebinding between that check and the connection, and a hostname the server cannot resolve itself (one only a proxy can resolve) is not checked.

The fetch tool will truncate the response, but by using the `start_index` argument, you can specify where to start the content extraction. This lets models read a webpage in chunks, until they find the information they need.

The markdown of an HTML page opens with the page's title as a `#` heading (its `og:title`, else its `` when the `<title>` holds it, else its `<title>` or ``), because the extraction drops a heading that repeats the title. It is not added when the markdown already opens with it, to a raw result, or to a page that failed to simplify.

### Available Tools

- `fetch` - Fetches a URL from the internet and extracts its contents as markdown.
    - `url` (string, required): URL to fetch
    - `max_length` (integer, optional): Maximum number of characters to return (default: 5000)
    - `start_index` (integer, optional): Start content from this character index (default: 0)
    - `raw` (boolean, optional): Get raw content without markdown conversion (default: false)
    - `timeout_ms` (integer, optional): HTTP request timeout for this call, in milliseconds, from 100 to 600000 (default: the server's timeout, 30000 unless configured; see [Customization - Timeout](#customization---timeout))
    - Annotations: `readOnlyHint: true`, `destructiveHint: false`, `idempotentHint: true`, `openWorldHint: true` (it only reads, and it reaches arbitrary hosts on the internet)

### Prompts

- **fetch**
  - Fetch a URL and extract its contents as markdown
  - Arguments:
    - `url` (string, required): URL to fetch

### Errors

- A failed fetch (a robots.txt refusal, an unreachable page, an HTTP error status, a refused private address, an unusable proxy setting, a response body over the [size limit](#response-size)) and arguments that do not match the tool's schema are returned as a tool result with `isError: true`, whose text starts `Error executing tool fetch:` and says what went wrong, so the model can read it and decide what to do.
- Calling a tool the server does not have is a JSON-RPC protocol error, `-32602` (`Unknown tool: <name>`), as the specification requires. So is getting a prompt it does not have (`Unknown prompt: <name>`), or the `fetch` prompt without its `url` (`URL is required`) or with a `url` that is not a valid URL (`Invalid URL '<url>': <reason>`).
- When the `fetch` prompt's fetch fails, the prompt still returns: its message holds the reason the fetch failed.

The server is built on the MCP Python SDK's high-level `MCPServer`: the tool and the prompt are decorated functions, and their type hints and field descriptions are the input schema and the prompt's arguments.

### Response size

The server reads at most 5 MiB (5,242,880 bytes) of a response body, so a very large or endless response cannot exhaust its memory. The limit is fixed and counts the body after its content encoding is decoded, and decoding itself stops at the limit, so a small compressed body that expands enormously is stopped without being expanded. The server asks for, and decodes, only `gzip` and `deflate` (`Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate`); a response in any other content encoding (`br`, `zstd`, or more than one encoding applied in turn) is refused with an error. A page whose `Content-Length` is over it is refused before any of the body is read; a page that streams past it is refused once it does. Either way the tool returns an error saying so (and the `fetch` prompt returns that message), rather than part of the page. A robots.txt over the limit is not refused: its rules are read from the first 5 MiB. Each redirect is followed without reading the redirect response's own body. `max_length` and `start_index` page through what was read, so they are not affected by this limit and do not raise it.

### Content negotiation

The tool and the prompt ask for markdown first, with the request header `Accept: text/markdown, text/html;q=0.9, */*;q=0.8`. A site that serves markdown through content negotiation sends it directly, and a `text/markdown` response is returned as-is: it is not simplified and carries no raw-content notice. A site that ignores the header sends what it always did, and HTML is simplified to markdown as before. A `raw` fetch keeps the default `Accept: */*`, so it gets whatever the site serves by default (for a web page, its HTML), unsimplified; a markdown response it receives anyway is returned as-is too.

### Protocol versions

The server speaks both eras of the Model Context Protocol over stdio, with nothing to configure: a **2026-07-28** client (discovered with `server/discover`, no session) and a **2025-11-25** client (the `initialize` handshake). The client's first request decides which. Tools and prompts behave the same in both. Methods the 2026-07-28 specification removes, such as `ping`, are answered only on a 2025-11-25 connection.

## Installation

readme.markdown:
# Knowledge Graph Memory Server

A basic implementation of persistent memory using a local knowledge graph. This lets Claude remember information about the user across chats.

Published on npm as [`@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory).

## Core Concepts

### Entities
Entities are the primary nodes in the knowledge graph. Each entity has:
- A unique name (identifier)
- An entity type (e.g., "person", "organization", "event")
- A list of observations

Example:
```json
{
  "name": "John_Smith",
  "entityType": "person",
  "observations": ["Speaks fluent Spanish"]
}
```

### Relations
Relations define directed connections between entities. They are always stored in active voice and describe how entities interact or relate to each other.

Example:
```json
{
  "from": "John_Smith",
  "to": "Anthropic",
  "relationType": "works_at"
}
```
### Observations
Observations are discrete pieces of information about an entity. They are:

- Stored as strings
- Attached to specific entities
- Can be added or removed independently
- Should be atomic (one fact per observation)

Example:
```json
{
  "entityName": "John_Smith",
  "observations": [
    "Speaks fluent Spanish",
    "Graduated in 2019",
    "Prefers morning meetings"
  ]
}
```

## API

### Tools
- **create_entities**
  - Create multiple new entities in the knowledge graph
  - Input: `entities` (array of objects)
    - Each object contains:
      - `name` (string): Entity identifier
      - `entityType` (string): Type classification
      - `observations` (string[]): Associated observations
  - Ignores entities with existing names (and repeats of a name earlier in the same call); their observations are not added
  - Returns the created entities. When any were skipped, the structured result also lists their names in `skipped`, and a second text item says which were skipped (use `add_observations` to extend an existing entity)

- **create_relations**
  - Create multiple new relations between entities
  - Input: `relations` (array of objects)
    - Each object contains:
      - `from` (string): Source entity name
      - `to` (string): Target entity name
      - `relationType` (string): Relationship type in active voice
  - Skips duplicate relations
  - Fails if either the source or target entity doesn't exist

- **add_observations**
  - Add new observations to existing entities
  - Input: `observations` (array of objects)
    - Each object contains:
      - `entityName` (string): Target entity
      - `contents` (string[]): New observations to add
  - Returns added observations per entity
  - Fails if entity doesn't exist

- **delete_entities**
  - Remove whole entities, with all their observations
  - Input: `entityNames` (string[])
  - Cascading deletion of every relation that points to or from a deleted entity
  - To remove a link between two entities and keep both, use `delete_relations`; to remove facts from an entity, use `delete_observations`
  - No error if an entity doesn't exist; the response reports which names were not found

- **delete_observations**
  - Remove specific observations from entities
  - Input: `deletions` (array of objects)
    - Each object contains:
      - `entityName` (string): Target entity
      - `observations` (string[]): Observations to remove
  - No error if an observation doesn't exist; the response reports how many were deleted

- **delete_relations**
  - Remove specific relations from the graph, keeping the entities they connect (to remove an entity itself, use `delete_entities`)
  - Input: `relations` (array of objects)
    - Each object contains:
      - `from` (string): Source entity name
      - `to` (string): Target entity name
      - `relationType` (string): Relationship type
  - A relation is deleted only when `from`, `to` and `relationType` all match a stored one exactly; read the stored `relationType` with `open_nodes` (or `search_nodes`) first if unsure
  - No error if a relation doesn't exist; the response reports how many were deleted

- **read_graph**
  - Read the entire knowledge graph
  - Optional input:
    - `entityTypes` (string[], at least one): return only entities of these types, and the relations that touch one of them
    - `observationLimit` (integer, 0 or more): see below
  - Returns complete graph structure with all entities and relations
  - With `observationLimit`, each entity carries at most that many observations (the first ones, in the order they were added) and an `observationCount` with its total. `observationLimit: 0` returns names, types and counts only: a cheap overview of a large graph, from which `open_nodes` reads the entities you need in full

- **search_nodes**
  - Search for nodes based on query
  - Input: `query` (string, at most 2048 characters; a longer query is rejected)
  - Searches across:
    - Entity names
    - Entity types
    - Observation content
  - Returns matching entities and their relations
  - Optional input:
    - `limit` (integer, 1 or more): return at most this many matches (the first, in stored order), with the relations that touch them
    - `observationLimit` (integer, 0 or more): as for `read_graph`

- **open_nodes**
  - Retrieve specific nodes by name
  - Input: `names` (string[])
  - Returns:
    - Requested entities
    - Relations between requested entities
  - Silently skips non-existent nodes
  - Optional input: `observationLimit` (integer, 0 or more), as for `read_graph`

### Resources

- **knowledge-graph** (`memory://knowledge-graph`)
  - The full knowledge graph as a readable MCP Resource
  - MIME type: `application/json`
  - Returns the same shape as `read_graph` (entities and relations)
  - Mutation tools (`create_entities`, `create_relations`, `add_observations`, `delete_entities`, `delete_observations`, `delete_relations`) emit `notifications/resources/updated` for this URI, so subscribed clients see live changes
  - How a client subscribes depends on its protoc

readme.markdown:
# Sequential Thinking MCP Server

An MCP server implementation that provides a tool for dynamic and reflective problem-solving through a structured thinking process.

Published on npm as [`@modelcontextprotocol/server-sequential-thinking`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@modelcontextprotocol/server-sequential-thinking).

## Features

- Break down complex problems into manageable steps
- Revise and refine thoughts as understanding deepens
- Branch into alternative paths of reasoning
- Adjust the total number of thoughts dynamically
- Generate and verify solution hypotheses
- Serves both protocol eras on stdio: 2026-07-28 clients (`server/discover`, no handshake) and 2025-era clients (`initialize`). The thought history lasts as long as the client's connection, on either era

## Tool

### sequentialthinking

Facilitates a detailed, step-by-step thinking process for problem-solving and analysis.

**Inputs:**
- `thought` (string): The current thinking step
- `nextThoughtNeeded` (boolean): Whether another thought step is needed
- `thoughtNumber` (integer): Current thought number
- `totalThoughts` (integer): Estimated total thoughts needed
- `isRevision` (boolean, optional): Whether this revises previous thinking
- `revisesThought` (integer, optional): Which thought is being reconsidered
- `branchFromThought` (integer, optional): Branching point thought number
- `branchId` (string, optional): Branch identifier
- `needsMoreThoughts` (boolean, optional): If more thoughts are needed

## Usage

The Sequential Thinking tool is designed for:
- Breaking down complex problems into steps
- Planning and design with room for revision
- Analysis that might need course correction
- Problems where the full scope might not be clear initially
- Tasks that need to maintain context over multiple steps
- Situations where irrelevant information needs to be filtered out

In practice, you do not call `sequentialthinking` directly by hand unless your client exposes raw tool calls. Instead, connect the server to an MCP-aware host and ask the model to think through a problem step by step. The host can then decide to call the tool one or more times while it works.

### What it looks like in use

Example prompts that typically benefit from this tool:

- `Plan a database migration from PostgreSQL 14 to 16, list risks, and revise the plan if downtime exceeds 5 minutes.`
- `Debug why this deployment only fails in production and show your reasoning step by step.`
- `Compare three architecture options for a file sync engine and branch if one assumption turns out to be wrong.`

### How to tell it is working

If your host or inspector shows tool activity, you should see repeated calls to `sequentialthinking` with fields such as:

- `thought`
- `thoughtNumber`
- `totalThoughts`
- `nextThoughtNeeded`

When the reasoning changes course, you may also see revision or branching fields like `isRevision`, `revisesThought`, `branchFromThought`, or `branchId`.

### Quick manual verification

After installing the server in your MCP host:

1. Restart or reload the host so it reconnects to the server.
2. Confirm the `sequentialthinking` tool appears in the host's MCP tool list or inspector.
3. Ask the host to solve a non-trivial problem in a step-by-step way.
4. Verify that the host invokes the tool multiple times instead of returning a one-shot answer.

## Requirements

Node.js 24 or later, when the server runs through `npx` or from source.

## Configuration

### Usage with Claude Desktop

Add this to your `claude_desktop_config.json`:

#### npx

```json
{

    "sequential-thinking": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "@modelcontextprotocol/server-sequential-thinking"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

On Windows, use `cmd /c` to launch `npx`:

      "command": "docker",

        "-i",

}
```

To disable logging of thought information set env var: `DISABLE_THOUGHT_LOGGING` to `true`.

Each thought is logged to stderr as a box, one row per line of the thought. The box is at most 100 characters wide, with longer lines (and a long branch ID in the header) wrapped, and draws at most 1000 rows of thought text; past that it ends with a row saying how many lines it left out. Only the log is shortened: the server keeps the whole thought in its history, and the tool result is unchanged.

To bound memory use, the server retains at most `MAX_THOUGHT_HISTORY` thoughts per connection (a positive integer; default `1000`). Past the cap the oldest thought is dropped, from its branch too, so `thoughtHistoryLength` in the result stops at the cap and a branch whose thoughts have all been dropped is no longer listed in `branches`.

# Time MCP Server

A Model Context Protocol server that provides time and timezone conversion capabilities. This server enables LLMs to get current time information and perform timezone conversions using IANA timezone names, with automatic system timezone detection.

Source: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/time

Requires MCP Python SDK 2.x (`mcp>=2.3,<3`).

### Available Tools

- `get_current_time` - Get current time in a specific timezone or system timezone.
  - Optional arguments:
    - `timezone` (string): IANA timezone name (e.g., 'America/New_York', 'Europe/London'). Defaults to the server's local timezone.

- `convert_time` - Convert time between timezones.
  - Required arguments:
    - `time` (string): Time in 24-hour format (HH:MM)
  - Optional arguments:
    - `source_timezone` (string): Source IANA timezone name. Defaults to the server's local timezone.
    - `target_timezone` (string): Target IANA timezone name. Defaults to the server's local timezone.

- `get_time_ago` - Get the time a given number of days, hours, minutes and seconds ago in a specific timezone, for questions such as "what happened in the last 5 hours?".
  - Optional arguments:
    - `timezone` (string): IANA timezone name; defaults to the server's local timezone
    - `days_ago`, `hours_ago`, `minutes_ago`, `seconds_ago` (non-negative JSON integers, default 0; a fraction, numeric string or boolean is rejected): how far back to go. They add up, so two and a half hours ago is `hours_ago: 2, minutes_ago: 30`.
  - The offset is elapsed time, counted back from the current instant, so across a daylight-saving change "a day ago" is exactly 24 hours ago and its wall-clock reading can differ from now by an hour. An offset reaching before year 1 is an error.

A timezone name, here and in `--local-timezone`, must be an exact IANA key, case included: `Europe/Warsaw` is accepted and `europe/warsaw` is rejected on every platform, including macOS, whose case-insensitive filesystem would otherwise resolve it.

### Protocol versions

The server speaks both eras of the Model Context Protocol over stdio, with nothing to configure: a **2026-07-28** client (discovered with `server/discover`, no session) and a **2025-11-25** client (the `initialize` handshake). The client's first request decides which. Tools behave the same in both. Methods the 2026-07-28 specification removes, such as `ping`, are answered only on a 2025-11-25 connection.

### Results and errors

The server is built on the SDK's high-level `MCPServer`. Each tool declares an `outputSchema` and returns its result twice: as `structuredContent`, and as the same object in indented JSON in a text block, for a client that does not read structured output.

- **A tool failure is an `isError` result** whose text the model can read and act on, prefixed `Error executing tool <name>: `. That covers an unknown or non-exact timezone (`Invalid timezone: ...`), an empty timezone (`Missing required argument: <argument>`), a time not in `HH:MM` 24-hour form, a wall-clock time skipped by a clock change, and an argument missing or of the wrong type (the SDK's validation message).
- **An ambiguous time is reported, not guessed.** On the day a clock change repeats a wall-clock time (a DST fall-back, such as 01:30 on 2024-11-03 in `America/New_York`), `convert_time` returns its first occurrence in `source` and `target`, and the second in `later_occurrence`: a `note` saying the time occurs twice, with that occurrence's own `source`, `target` and `time_difference`. For any other time `later_occurrence` is `null`.
- **An unknown tool name is a JSON-RPC `-32602` error** (`Unknown tool: <name>`), not an `isError` result, as both protocol versions specify.
- The server registers no prompts or resources. Their list methods answer with empty lists.

## Installation

### Using uv (recommended)

When using [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) no specific installation is needed. We will

```bash

```

### Using PIP

Alternatively you can install `mcp-server-time` via pip:

# Everything MCP Server

**[Architecture](docs/architecture.md)
| [Project Structure](docs/structure.md)
| [Startup Process](docs/startup.md)
| [Server Features](docs/features.md)
| [Extension Points](docs/extension.md)
| [How It Works](docs/how-it-works.md)**

This MCP server attempts to exercise all the features of the MCP protocol. It is not intended to be a useful server, but rather a test server for builders of MCP clients. It implements prompts, tools, resources, sampling, and more to showcase MCP capabilities.

## Tools, Resources, Prompts, and Other Features

A complete list of the registered MCP primitives and other protocol features demonstrated can be found in the [Server Features](docs/features.md) document.

The resource collections (`demo://resource/collection/summer-specials`, and the `by-category/{category}` and `item/{itemId}` templates beside it) show a single `resources/read` returning several contents, each under its own URI: reading a collection returns one content per item, and each item's URI can be read on its own.

The server info and every tool, prompt, resource and resource template carry a pair of [icons](docs/features.md#icons), one for a light theme and one for a dark theme, so a client can show the variant that suits its own background.

The `get-env` tool returns the server's environment variables, but masks the value of any credential-like name (a `KEY`, `TOKEN`, `SECRET`, `PASSWORD`, `PASSWD`, `CREDENTIAL`, `AUTH` or `COOKIE` segment, such as `OPENAI_API_KEY`) as `"<redacted>"`. To see every value unmasked while debugging, start the server with `GET_ENV_INCLUDE_SECRETS=1` (or `true`). Leave it unset otherwise: with it set, every credential in the server's environment reaches the model's context.

## Protocol versions

The server serves both protocol eras, over stdio and Streamable HTTP, from one process:

- **2026-07-28** clients connect with `server/discover`, send their protocol version, identity and capabilities with each request, and have no session. The server demonstrates the revision's new features for them: multi-round-trip requests (`input_required`) with `requestState`, `subscriptions/listen` change notifications, per-request log levels, cache hints (`ttlMs` / `cacheScope`), the tasks extension (`io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks`) under the `extensions` capability, and `x-mcp-header` with JSON Schema 2020-12 tool schemas.
- **2025-era** clients connect with the `initialize` handshake, as before. Elicitation, sampling and roots are served to them from the same multi-round-trip handlers through the SDK's legacy shim.

Roots, sampling and logging are deprecated as of 2026-07-28 and stay available, labelled deprecated. [Server Features](docs/features.md) marks which era each feature belongs to.

## Configuring `gzip-file-as-resource`

The `gzip-file-as-resource` tool fetches the URL it is given, so these environment variables limit what it will fetch:

| Variable | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GZIP_MAX_FETCH_SIZE` | 10 MiB | The largest response, in bytes, it reads |
| `GZIP_MAX_FETCH_TIME_MILLIS` | 30000 | How long a fetch may take, redirects included |
| `GZIP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` | empty (any name) | Comma-separated host names; a host must be one of them or a subdomain of one. Checked on the caller's URL and on every redirect hop |
| `GZIP_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS` | off | Set to `1` or `true` to allow loopback, private (RFC 1918), CGNAT, link-local (cloud metadata) and other non-public addresses |

By default the tool refuses a URL whose host resolves to a non-public address, and follows at most five redirects, checking each hop the same way. `GZIP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` filters names, not addresses: a listed name that resolves to a private address is still refused unless `GZIP_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS` is set. The address is checked before the request and resolved again when it is made, so a DNS answer that changes in between (DNS rebinding) is not caught. `data:` URLs are not fetched, so neither check applies to them.

## Requirements

Node.js 24 or later, when the server runs through `npx` or from source.

## Usage with Claude Desktop (uses [stdio Transport](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/basic/transports#stdio))

# Worklittle Jobs

Find jobs near you and apply to them instantly. Worklittle searches over 7.5 million job listings with filters like visa status, distance and salary, recommends the ones that fit you, and applies to one or several at once from your Worklittle account.

Public MCP connector and plugin files for [Worklittle](https://worklittle.com). This repository contains skill instructions, a plugin manifest, and a pointer to the public MCP URL. It does not contain API keys, OAuth secrets, or private product source.

## What users get

- Remote MCP at `https://mcp.worklittle.com/`
- Search with visa, distance, salary, and other filters
- Connect a Worklittle account to apply to one or several jobs instantly and save jobs

## Connect

Remote Streamable HTTP (any MCP client):

```
https://mcp.worklittle.com/
```

Add that URL in ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor, Claude, Codex, or another app that supports remote MCP. Docs for each client: https://docs.worklittle.com/mcp

Claude Code (this is the Claude CLI, not the connector name):

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http worklittle https://mcp.worklittle.com/
```

Docs: https://docs.worklittle.com/mcp  
Privacy: https://worklittle.com/privacy  
Support: hello@worklittle.com

## Client manifests

The same remote MCP and skills work in Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Codex, and other clients. Each host just looks for its own files:

- Claude Code / Claude plugin directory: `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`
- Cursor Marketplace: `.cursor-plugin/` plus `mcp.json` (Cursor’s required filename)
- Official MCP Registry: `server.json`
- Skills (`npx skills add`): `skills/`

Cursor’s reviewer script is in this repo so a marketplace submit matches their [plugin template](https://github.com/cursor/plugin-template). It does not make this a Cursor-only project.

```bash
node scripts/validate-template.mjs
```

## Agent skills

Install the public job-search skills into Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, and other agents:

```bash
npx skills add worklittle/jobs-mcp
```

Browse them on [skills.sh](https://skills.sh). Docs also publish skills at `https://docs.worklittle.com`.

## License

MIT

## Directories

Listed in the [Claude Market MCP directory](https://www.claudemarket.ai/mcp).

# Achromat MCP server

An [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server that lets any MCP host (Claude Desktop, an IDE, an agent framework) use [Achromat Machine Operational Memory (MOM)](https://achromat.ai) as native tools. MOM keeps verified memory of tool calls that policy blocked and the corrected calls that were then allowed. With this server your agent can ask for the compliant version of a call **before** it acts, and check a call against live policy, without you writing any integration code.

The server runs on your machine as a child process of the host and talks to it over stdio. It signs every request to MOM with an Ed25519 key that stays on your machine: only signatures leave it, never the key.

## Add it to Claude Desktop

Open the configuration file:

| OS | Path |
| --- | --- |
| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` |
| Windows | `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` |

Add the server under `mcpServers`, then restart Claude Desktop:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "achromat": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@achromat-ai/mcp-server"]
    }
  }
}
```

That is the whole setup. Requires Node.js 20 or newer; `-y` lets `npx` install the package without asking. Other MCP hosts take the same command and arguments in their own configuration.

## First use: your agent sets up the identity

Every request to MOM is signed, so the server needs a key that MOM knows. You do not create or register one yourself. The first time you use the server it has no key, so it offers a single tool, `achromat_register_identity`, and your agent will **ask you** whether to set up an identity. If you say yes, the server:

1. generates an Ed25519 key pair on your machine,
2. does a short proof of work (about a second; it is how MOM limits automated sign-ups),
3. registers the **public** key with MOM, and
4. saves the **private** key to `~/.achromat/achromat_agent_key.pem`, readable only by you.

Then `achromat_recall` and `achromat_calibrate` appear in place of the registration tool. If your host does not refresh its tool list by itself, restart it once.

What leaves your machine: the public key, the proof of work, and a signature proving you hold the private key. The private key never does. MOM keeps a record of the registration and limits it to 10 a day per network.

**The key file is the identity.** Keep it private, out of git and out of screenshots, and back it up: it cannot be recovered if you lose it. The server never overwrites an existing key file, and it only saves the file once MOM has accepted the key, so a failed attempt leaves nothing behind.

## Choosing where the key lives

By default the key is at `~/.achromat/achromat_agent_key.pem`. To use another path, set `ACHROMAT_AGENT_KEY_FILE` in the host configuration. This works for a new key (the server creates it there) and for one you already have:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "achromat": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@achromat-ai/mcp-server"],
      "env": {
        "ACHROMAT_AGENT_KEY_FILE": "/Users/you/keys/achromat_agent_key.pem"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

On Windows use the full path with escaped backslashes, for example `"C:\\Users\\you\\keys\\achromat_agent_key.pem"`. A leading `~` is expanded by the server. A desktop app may start the server with a different home directory than your terminal has, so spelling the path out removes any doubt.

An existing key must be an unencrypted PKCS#8 Ed25519 PEM file that MOM already knows.

## Attributing an install to a link (optional)

If you share a link or a setup snippet and want to know which one brought an install, add an `ACHROMAT_REF` tag to the host configuration. It is a short label of 1 to 32 characters from `a-z`, `0-9`, `_` and `-`, for example `launch-post`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "achromat": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@achromat-ai/mcp-server"],
      "env": { "ACHROMAT_REF": "launch-post" }
    }
  }
}
```

The tag is sent only while the server registers its identity, as `?ref=launch-post` on the two registration calls, and nowhere else. It is the label itself and nothing about you or your machine. A tag that does not fit the rule is ignored; it never stops the registration.

## Run from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/achromat-ai/achromat-mcp-server.git
cd achromat-mcp-server
npm install
npm run build
```

Point the host at the build instead of `npx`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "achromat": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/absolute/path/to/achromat-mcp-server/dist/index.js"]
    }
  }
}
```

To try the tools in a browser without a host, use the MCP Inspector:

```bash
npm run inspect
```

## Tools

### `achromat_register_identity`

Offered only while there is no key file. Creates and registers an identity as described above. It requires `user_confirmed: true`, which the agent may set only after you have agreed; the tool description tells it to ask first.

| Parameter | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `user_confirmed` | yes | Must be `true`, and only after the user has said yes. |

### `achromat_recall`

Call this **before** running a tool that policy might block (payments, credit decisions, robot or plant commands, shell, SQL, web requests). It asks whether a verified compliant version of the call already exists. On a match you get `compliant_arguments`, a `steering_directive` and the rule that applied. Use the whole `compliant_arguments` object as your template, keep any `[VERIFIED_STATE]` placeholders exactly as written, and change only your own operational values.

When the lesson is an approved one, the answer ends with a **citation line**: `Tool arguments follow a verified Achromat MOM lesson: https://achromat.ai/?ref=audit#lesson-<id>`. The agent is told to add it to text a person reads (its final answer, a pull request description, a commit message), never to the tool's arguments, and to skip it if you ask for no attribu

# AISTLabs MCP server

Generate video, images and audio on top AI models from your agent — with an AI director built in.

AISTLabs is an AI creative studio for agents. Connect it to Claude, ChatGPT, Codex or any MCP client and create video, images and audio right from the chat — short films, social content, music videos, ads or anything you imagine.

- **Top models in one place.** Seedance 2.5, Wan 3.0, MiniMax, Nano Banana, GPT Image, Seedream, ElevenLabs voices and music. Drafts in 480p, finals in 1080p; references, first and last frames, video editing.
- **AI director.** Describe an idea or share a photo. AISTLabs writes the script, directs and renders a finished video.
- **Price before you spend.** Every generation is quoted in credits first; your agent asks before spending.
- **Your library.** Projects, history, favourites and reusable elements: characters, locations, props.
- **For brands.** Brand Brain remembers your style and products; performance ads turn a winning creative into variations to test.

**Built for agents:** clear tool descriptions, idempotent creation, live status, confirmation before deleting, and errors that say what to do next.

**Connect:** one-click OAuth 2.1 sign-in, or an API key from aistlabs.ai/connect-agent. Connecting is free; generations use AISTLabs credits, and new accounts get 20 free credits.

## Connect

**Endpoint:** `https://aistlabs.ai/mcp` (Streamable HTTP, OAuth 2.1)

- **Claude:** Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector → paste `https://aistlabs.ai/mcp` → sign in.
- **Cursor and other MCP clients:**
  ```json
  { "mcpServers": { "aistlabs": { "url": "https://aistlabs.ai/mcp" } } }
  ```
- **API key instead of OAuth:** create one at https://aistlabs.ai/connect-agent and send `Authorization: Bearer <key>`.

## Example prompts

1. Make a 10-second cinematic shot of a dragon flying over a neon city at night, 16:9.
2. Turn my photo into a Pixar-style character and animate a 5-second clip.
3. Write and voice a 20-second intro for my YouTube channel.
4. Turn this product photo into a 15-second vertical ad for TikTok.
5. How much would a 10-second Seedance 2.5 video in 1080p cost?

## Docs

https://aistlabs.ai/docs/index.md · Privacy: https://aistlabs.ai/privacy · Terms: https://aistlabs.ai/terms · Support: support@aistlabs.ai

readme.markdown:
# SpotDB

### Lightweight data sandbox for AI workflows and data exploration, enabled with guardrails and security to keep your data safe.

This project provides a lightweight, **ephemeral data sandbox** designed for large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows. By providing a secure, isolated environment, it allows AI agents and scripts to analyze data without direct access to production databases. This setup prevents accidental data modification, ensures data privacy, and enforces guardrails for safe data exploration.

## Features

- 🏖️ **Ephemeral Data Sandbox**: Create temporary databases for AI workflows and data exploration.
- 📸 **Snapshot**: Capture and store data snapshots, recover point-in-time data states or continue from a previous state.
- 🧠 **MCP API**: Access data through a Model Context Protocol for seamless integration with AI models and agentic workflows.
- ⚙️ **REST API**: Access data through a RESTful API for integration with traditional systems and workflows.
- 🚂 **Guardrails**: Enforce rules and constraints to ensure data safety and privacy.
- 🛡️ **Security**: Protect data from unauthorized access and modification.

## Quick Start

1. Tap the repository and install the package:

```bash
brew tap aliengiraffe/spaceship && \\
brew install spotdb
```

2. Start the server:

```bash
spotdb
```

3. Upload a CSV file:

```bash
curl -X POST \
  http://localhost:8080/api/v1/upload \
  -F "table_name=mytable" \
  -F "has_header=true" \
  -F "csv_file=@data.csv"
```

4. Query the data:

```bash
curl -X POST \
  http://localhost:8080/api/v1/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "SELECT * FROM mytable LIMIT 10"}'
```

5. Setup Claude Code
   You must have the `claude` command installed.

Then, you can add the `spotdb` mcp:

```bash
claude mcp add spotdb -s user -- npx -y mcp-remote http://localhost:8081/stream
```

## Use Explorer UI

Open the Explorer UI in your browser and upload files and query the data:

```bash
open http://localhost:8080/explorer
```

## Full Documentation

👉 [https://github.com/aliengiraffe/spotdb/blob/main/DOCS.md](https://github.com/aliengiraffe/spotdb/blob/main/DOCS.md)

# Analytics Legends — SAP AI & Analytics MCP Server A **read-only** [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server over a curated corpus of the **SAP AI & analytics services market**: who delivers SAP Business AI and Joule, Business Data Cloud, SAP Datasphere, SAP Analytics Cloud and BW/4HANA work, what the contract market looks like, what the day rates are, what the vocabulary means, and what has just happened. It exists so that an assistant answering an SAP analytics question can **cite a record instead of guessing**. Every row carries a `citation_url` on analyticslegends.ai, and every response carries the size of the population it was drawn from. **Nothing to install.** The server is hosted: ``` https://analyticslegends.ai/mcp streamable-http ``` The public tools need no credential. Looking for an MCP server that connects to your **own** SAP system (BTP, CAP, UI5, Fiori, ABAP, Datasphere…)? This one serves market data, not your tenant — the [catalogue of SAP MCP servers](https://analyticslegends.ai/guides/sap-mcp-servers/) lists the official SAP, AWS and community servers, verified on their own pages. --- ## Connect
Claude Code ```bash claude mcp add --transport http analytics-legends https://analyticslegends.ai/mcp # with a subscriber key, to open the eight gated tools: claude mcp add --transport http analytics-legends https://analyticslegends.ai/mcp \ --header "Authorization: Bearer alk_…" ```
Claude web, Desktop and mobile (custom connector) Add a custom connector pointing at `https://analyticslegends.ai/mcp`. The public tranche answers immediately, with no credential. To open the paid tranche, use the connector's **request-header authentication** and set `Authorization` to `Bearer alk_…`. The credential is entered once, by whoever adds the connector, and is shared by that workspace — one key, one daily quota. There is no OAuth consent flow to walk: this server's unit of access is a personal API key minted on an analyticslegends.ai account, not a delegated identity.
Claude Desktop / any client reading a JSON config ```json { "mcpServers": { "analytics-legends": { "type": "streamable-http", "url": "https://analyticslegends.ai/mcp" } } } ```
With a subscriber key (opens the eight gated tools) ```json { "mcpServers": { "analytics-legends": { "type": "streamable-http", "url": "https://analyticslegends.ai/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer alk_…" } } } } ```
The manifest is served at [`/.well-known/mcp.json`](https://analyticslegends.ai/.well-known/mcp.json) and mirrored in this repository as [`mcp.json`](./mcp.json). `tools/list` is the authority for the surface — this README is a copy, and a copy can drift. --- ## The 22 tools **Fourteen are public and unauthenticated.** Eight need a subscriber key; they are **listed and refuse by name**, never hidden — an agent can see what it is missing. Three open at Consultant, five at Legend, and the MCP Pass opens all eight. | Tool | Answers | |---|---| | `search_firms` | Which SAP analytics providers match a country, kind, free text | | `count_firms_by` | A counting question in one call, instead of a page of rows | | `get_firm` | One organisation from the published directory | | `list_firm_kinds` | The directory's breakdown by organisation kind, with live counts | | `find_opportunities` | The live contract and permanent-role radar | | `search_news` | The curated SAP analytics news corpus | | `search_concepts` | The concept encyclopaedia — the vocabulary of the stack | | `get_concept` | One concept: title, category, level, tags, editor's summary | | `list_studies` | The deep-research study editions and their metadata | | `get_day_rate_benchmark` | The public day-rate aggregate by country, stack, seniority | | `list_sap_modules` | The canonical SAP module/product taxonomy | | `list_freelance_platforms` | The CV/profile platforms a consultant can sign up on | | `find_academy_modules` | The Academy training catalogue, searchable by module | | `query_knowledge_graph` | A traversal of the learning knowledge graph | | 🔒 `get_concept_card` | The full encyclopaedia card — body, key points, cheat sheet | | 🔒 `get_study` | One study **body** | | 🔒 `get_academy_module` | One Academy module, in full | | 🔒 `find_sap_clients` | The SAP end-customer corpus — who *runs* SAP | | 🔒 `get_sap_client_profile` | One end-customer's SAP footprint and analytics estate | | 🔒 `get_firm_intel` | A firm's practice size, partner level, delivery flags | | 🔒 `get_expansion_brief` | Before opening in another region: providers, SAP end-customers and openings there, and the brand families bridging your home region to it | | 🔒 `find_partner_candidates` | The local providers of a target country or region to partner with, subcontract to, or acquire | Every tool is annotated `readOnlyHint: true`. The server writes nothing, anywhere. --- ## Two rules it holds itself to **A count is read at query time, and it comes with its population.** Responses carry `_meta.match_count` (what your filters matched) and `_meta.tranche_total_row_count` (the whole tranche). Quote those rather than any number written in a description — including the ones in this file. **A citation says what it is.** Every item carries `citation_url` **and** `citation_scope`. `record` means the URL is that item's own page; `section_hub` means this platform publishes no page for that item and the URL is the section index — say so, or cite the section, but do not present a hub URL as the item's page. News items also carry `source_url` for the upstream publisher: cite both. --- ## What is deliberately **not** served, at any tier - **People.** Individual professionals are held as initials only. readme.markdown:
# Atlaso — remote MCP server

**Atlaso is an AI memory layer: one shared, persistent memory across every AI tool you connect.**

Tell it once in one tool, and it's already there in the next. Atlaso recalls the
context that matters before each turn and captures the durable facts after — your
decisions, your preferences, and where you left off.

This repository documents Atlaso's **hosted MCP server**. Atlaso is a managed
service, so there is nothing to self-host and no server code here — you connect
to the endpoint below and authorize in your browser.

- **Endpoint:** `https://mcp.atlaso.ai/mcp`
- **Transport:** Streamable HTTP
- **Auth:** OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration — your MCP client walks you
  through it; there are no API keys to paste
- **Website:** https://www.atlaso.ai
- **Docs:** https://docs.atlaso.ai

## Why this exists
Claude Desktop, Zed, Cline and other MCP clients have no memory of their own that reaches your coding tools. This hosted server gives any MCP client the same memory your coding tools share: decisions made in long chats, research and notes, preferences that should follow you. Memory works when the model calls the tools (remember, recall, forget); a skill can make that routine. Add `https://mcp.atlaso.ai/mcp` as a connector and sign in. [Claude Desktop](https://www.atlaso.ai/for/claude-desktop) · [Any MCP tool](https://docs.atlaso.ai/tools/custom-mcp)

## Connect

Any MCP client that supports remote servers can connect. Add
`https://mcp.atlaso.ai/mcp` as a connector and authorize in the browser when
prompted.

**Claude Desktop / claude.ai** — Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector →
paste the endpoint → Connect → authorize.

**Cursor, VS Code, and other MCP clients** — add it as a remote MCP server:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "atlaso": {
      "url": "https://mcp.atlaso.ai/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

**Terminal-based tools** (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity) get a richer
integration than MCP alone — automatic recall before each turn and automatic
capture after, via hooks. One command sets all of them up:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://atlaso.ai/install.sh | bash    # macOS / Linux
irm https://atlaso.ai/install.ps1 | iex           # Windows
```

That installs the `atlaso` CLI, links the machine (creating your account if you
don't have one), then asks which of your AI tools should share the memory.

## Tools

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `recall(query, limit=5)` | Search your memory for notes relevant to `query`. Returns a ranked list of `{id, content}`. Read-only. |
| `remember(text, polarity)` | Save a durable note — a decision, preference, or gotcha. `polarity` is one of `positive`, `open`, `cautionary`, `negative`. Returns the new id. |
| `recent(limit=10)` | List the most recent memories, newest first. Read-only. |
| `forget(id)` | Permanently delete a memory by id. Destructive and not undoable. |
| `status()` | Connection state, how many memories are stored and pending, and your memory health score. Read-only. |

Every recall carries a verdict on whether a memory is settled or contested, so
the model isn't acting on shaky context.

## Memory scopes

Memories are either **personal** (they follow you everywhere) or **project**
(scoped to the repository or workspace you were in). Both are recalled
automatically in the right place — you don't manage scopes by hand.

## Privacy

Secrets are scrubbed before anything is stored. Data is encrypted in transit and
at rest. Your memory is never used to train AI models and never sold. On the free
plan it is never sent to any LLM at all. You can delete any single memory, or your
whole account, at any time.

## Pricing

Free for one device and one tool. Pro is **$10/month** for unlimited devices and
tools sharing one memory, plus Ambient Memory, background enrichment, Ask your
memory, and JSON export. Build is **$25/month** and adds a developer memory API.

## Registry

Listed in the official MCP Registry as `io.github.imashishkh21/atlaso`. The
[`server.json`](./server.json) in this repository is the published manifest.

---

Atlaso is a product of Atlaso Labs Inc. This repository is documentation for the
hosted service; the service itself is not open source.

# Bowmark skill: live, structured data from 750+ websites for your agent

Ask for prices, listings, profiles or reviews by name (Amazon, LinkedIn, YouTube,
Airbnb and more) and get typed results back. Every account starts with a free $10.

<sub>**LM Studio**: GitHub strips a raw `lmstudio:` link, so this one is a paste, not a button. Copy it into your browser's address bar:</sub>

```
lmstudio://add_mcp?name=bowmark&config=eyJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL2FwaS5ib3dtYXJrLmFpL21jcC9iYWRnZS1sbXN0dWRpbyJ9
```

The skill for [Bowmark](https://bowmark.ai), the web as callable functions. The agent reads a typed function library, writes a short script against it, and Bowmark runs it on the live sites.

Jigs: small pages built on Bowmark and published for anyone to use. Each one runs with your own logins on the sites it lists, and your agent can search, open and publish them. Browse the store at https://bowmark.ai/jigs.

```sh
npx skills add bowmark-ai/skill
```

Works on any host that supports the `SKILL.md` standard — **Claude Code, Codex** (which adopted the standard natively), Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and others.

The skill calls Bowmark's MCP server — wire that up at [bowmark.ai/#install](https://bowmark.ai/#install) or via [Smithery](https://smithery.ai/servers/bowmark-ai/bowmark).

**Want both in one step?** On Claude Code and Codex, install the plugin instead — it bundles this skill *and* auto-wires the MCP:

```sh
# Claude Code
claude plugin marketplace add bowmark-ai/plugin && claude plugin install bowmark@bowmark-ai
# Codex
codex plugin marketplace add bowmark-ai/plugin   # then `codex /plugins` to install
```

## Tools

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `get_library` | Read the typed function library for a task or a site. Read-only, touches no site, and an unrecognized query returns the index rather than an error. |
| `run` | Execute a short async JavaScript script against the live sites and return `{ ok, result, logs, error, ms }`. |
| `report` | Tell Bowmark what it could not do, or which run came back wrong. Recorded as feedback; retries nothing. |

**No MCP client?** The same two calls are plain HTTP — `GET https://api.bowmark.ai/v1/library?query=…` and `POST https://api.bowmark.ai/v1/run`, both taking `Authorization: Bearer $BOWMARK_API_KEY`. The reference is [bowmark.ai/docs/api](https://bowmark.ai/docs/api); worked examples are at [bowmark.ai/docs/scripting#no-install-at-all](https://bowmark.ai/docs/scripting#no-install-at-all).

## OpenAI Apps (ChatGPT plugin) variant

The [ChatGPT Apps](https://platform.openai.com/plugins) submission takes a skill as a **ZIP or folder**, and its needs differ slightly from the general skill: the plugin always ships the MCP alongside the skill, and ChatGPT exposes the tools under bare names. So there's a tailored variant, **generated from this same canonical skill** — never hand-maintained:

- **Folder:** [`openai/bowmark/`](./openai/bowmark) — a content mirror of `bowmark/SKILL.md` with the trailing "Your API key" section and everything after it dropped (ChatGPT signs in by OAuth and cannot send a key), tool names rewritten to bare `get_library` / `run`, Claude-only frontmatter/tool-name references trimmed, and the three secret tools (`list_secrets`, `request_secret`, `get_secret_link`) replaced by the dashboard — the plugin's MCP is the ChatGPT directory connector, which does not offer them. That step refuses to build if the canonical wording moves out from under it. `build-openai.mjs` is the authority on what it cuts; this line described sections that have never existed in `bowmark/SKILL.md`, and a newcomer went looking for one.
- **ZIP:** [`openai/bowmark-openai-skill.zip`](./openai/bowmark-openai-skill.zip) — the same folder zipped, ready to drop straight into the ChatGPT "Skills" uploader. A **committed artifact** (not built in CI: the release runner has no `zip` binary), so it rides the mirror to `bowmark-ai/skill` at a stable raw URL like any other file.

Both are **generated** by [`build-openai.mjs`](./build-openai.mjs). Edit `bowmark/SKILL.md`, then regenerate and commit — never edit the `openai/` copies directly (CI's `check:openai` fails a PR whose text mirror is stale):

```sh
pnpm -F @bowmark/skill sync:openai        # regenerate openai/bowmark/SKILL.md
pnpm -F @bowmark/skill build:openai-zip    # rebuild openai/bowmark-openai-skill.zip (commit it)
```

# brainattic MCP server

**The knowledge base your AI reads and writes — under your rules.**

Valuable knowledge gets scattered across private AI conversations, individual assistants and
disconnected systems. brainattic gives people and AI agents a shared, persistent, governed
knowledge base: one authoritative set of versioned documents, even when teammates use different
AI clients. Human-defined permissions control access, rules guide how agents work, and revision
history makes changes traceable and recoverable.

brainattic is not another AI chatbot, a chat-history archive, or a replacement for SharePoint,
Git or your existing business systems. It holds the knowledge your team needs across them:
decisions, procedures, customer context and project history. AI clients connect over the
[Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) to search, read and update it.

This repository documents the hosted brainattic MCP server: what it does, how to connect a
client, and how to use it. It contains no server code. The service is hosted and operated by
Finite Software Systems Ltd.

| | |
|---|---|
| MCP endpoint | `https://app.brainattic.ai/api/mcp` |
| Transport | Streamable HTTP |
| Authentication | OAuth 2.1, discovered automatically (dynamic client registration, no API key or client secret) |
| Official MCP Registry name | `ai.brainattic/knowledge-base` |
| Discovery card | <https://brainattic.ai/.well-known/mcp/server.json> |
| Product and sign-up | <https://brainattic.ai> |
| Connect guide | <https://brainattic.ai/docs/connect> |
| Support | <https://brainattic.ai/support> · hello@brainattic.ai |

## One knowledge base, every agent

Personal AI memory helps one person in one client. Shared knowledge lets the whole team build
on a decision, correct it once and carry it into the next task without copying private chats
or asking everyone to switch assistants.

Sales can work in ChatGPT, analysts in Claude, developers in VS Code with GitHub Copilot, and
operations in Hermes. Each uses the same versioned knowledge, within their own permissions,
while keeping their preferred tools and workflow.

Three distinct mechanisms keep that collaboration governed:

- **Permissions** enforce what each user and their connected agent may access or modify.
- **Rules** are human-authored instructions for how agents should work. They guide behaviour;
  they are not technically enforced access controls or a substitute for permissions.
- **Revisions and auditability** make changes traceable, support review, and let you recover
  earlier document versions.

We built brainattic at Finite Software Systems Ltd to close exactly that gap in our own work. See
**[One knowledge base, every agent](docs/team-workflow.md)** for a change request followed from
the customer call through analysis, implementation, testing and shipping, and for how a new
team member gets up to speed in a single conversation.

## What the server does

When you connect, your agent works inside your brainattic workspace with your own permissions.
Each person signs in with their own account, so an agent can only reach what that person can.

The tools fall into these groups:

- **Search and retrieval.** Hybrid keyword and semantic search across documents, plus passage
  retrieval for grounded answers with citations.
- **Documents.** Create, read, list and update Markdown documents. Edits can be precise: open
  an edit session, apply changes in a batch, then commit or discard them.
- **Revisions.** Every saved change is a revision. List the history, read any past revision, and
  restore an earlier one.
- **Rules.** Human-written workspace, project and group instructions that agents should read
  before writing, to guide changes according to your team's conventions.
- **Projects and groups.** Organise documents, and archive or restore them.
- **Attachments.** Attach files and images to documents, and view them.
- **Skills.** Store reusable agent procedures as versioned skills with supporting files.
- **Reminders.** Set one-off or recurring reminders for workspace members.

Your client discovers the current tool list when it connects. Every tool carries MCP
annotations (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`, `openWorldHint`), so clients can ask before
running a tool that changes or deletes data.

## Data security and hosting

Core customer data is stored and processed on infrastructure controlled by Finite Software
Systems Ltd in **Bulgaria, European Union**. Finite Software Systems Ltd operates its own
infrastructure, colocated in a **Tier 3+ data centre in Sofia**. The data-centre operator
provides the physical facility and its access controls, with no logical access to customer data.

Customer workspaces have logical tenant isolation, role-based permissions and individual
user authentication. Access is protected by TLS; MCP connections use OAuth-based
authentication. Finite Software Systems Ltd uses segmented networks, firewalls, restricted
administrative access, operational and security logging and monitoring, and regular backups
on EU infrastructure under its control. Finite Software Systems Ltd strictly follows its
documented ISO 9001 and ISO/IEC 27001 procedures.

brainattic does not independently forward customer documents to third-party AI models.
Your chosen AI client can receive content you explicitly request through the connector,
subject to your permissions and that client's own policies. EU hosting does not determine
where your AI provider processes that content. Optional integrations, such as Slack reminders,
can also involve transfers outside the EEA; the published policies describe these and other
limited exceptions.

For the published security measures, data-handling details and contractual commitments, see
[Security](https://brainattic.ai/security), the [Privacy Policy](https://brainattic.ai/privacy)
and the [Data Processing Agreement](https://brainattic.ai/dpa).

readme.markdown:
Brain Memory

  
  
  

A hierarchical, file-system-based memory plugin for AI coding agents. Inspired by human neuroscience — memories are organized into deep nested life-domain categories, connected via associative networks, strengthened through spaced recall, and naturally decay over time.

One hosted **MCP connector** reaches every major agent and chat app — **Claude Code**, **OpenAI Codex CLI**, **OpenCode**, **GitHub Copilot CLI**, **Kilo**, the **Claude.ai** apps, **ChatGPT**, **Google Antigravity** (Gemini CLI's successor), **OpenClaw** / **NVIDIA NemoClaw**, **Hermes Agent**, and **Goose**. Prefer a free, local-first install? The native plugin runs entirely from `~/.brain/` on Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Kilo, and Antigravity — and dedicated [native integrations](integrations/) plug the same brain into OpenClaw and Hermes as their memory engine.

```
~/.brain/
├── professional/
│   └── companies/
│       └── acme-corp/
│           └── projects/
│               └── alpha-launch.md        ⚡ 0.88
├── personal/
│   └── education/
│       └── typescript-generics.md         ⚡ 0.72
├── social/
│   └── communities/
│       └── open-source-contrib.md         ⚡ 0.65
└── family/
    └── events/
        └── annual-reunion-planning.md     ⚡ 0.55
```

## Why Brain Memory?

Existing AI memory solutions use flat databases with tag-based retrieval. Brain Memory is different:

- **The directory tree IS the semantic structure** — `professional/companies/acme/projects/` tells the agent everything about context without vector search
- **Human-inspectable** — Browse your "brain" in any file explorer
- **Git-friendly** — Full version history of how memories evolve
- **Strength + decay** — Recalled memories get stronger, forgotten ones fade. Just like your brain
- **Recall receipts** — Memory that visibly fires: every answer shaped by a memory ends with a one-line attributable receipt (`◉ memory: "<title>" (<type>, <age>)`), minted by the engine so it can't be hallucinated
- **Provenance-bounded trust** — Every memory records where it came from (`user`, `agent-inferred`, `tool-output`, `external`), and recall weighs it: a fact planted by a web page or tool output is down-ranked, flagged `low_trust`, marked `⚠` on its receipt, and can never outrank what you said directly — no matter how many copies of it get written. And because memories are plain files, Brain records a **SHA-256 baseline** of each one at write time — so `brain audit` also catches a memory edited *outside* any write path, the one poisoning route every write-path defense is blind to
- **Bitemporal — it knows *when* a fact was true** — Every memory separates record time (when the brain learned it) from valid time (`valid_from` / `valid_until`, when it was actually true). So "we deploy to Fly.io" and "we deploy to Render" aren't a contradiction to guess between — they're one fact with a boundary. `brain recall "deploy target" --as-of 2026-03-01` answers what was true in March; `--as-known-of` answers what the brain knew then. Facts that stopped being true are demoted and marked `⌛ expired`, never silently served as current
- **Deterministic recall — every agent ranks identically** — Scoring is arithmetic over files, not a model call: TF-IDF/BM25 relevance, decayed strength, spreading activation, context match, salience. Claude, Codex, and Gemini asking the same question of the same brain get the *same* ranking, in the same order, offline. No embedding-model version can silently reshuffle what your agent remembers
- **Associative network** — Memories link to each other with weighted connections. Recalling one activates related ones automatically
- **Context-dependent recall** — Memories encoded in a similar context to the current session are scored higher
- **Spaced reinforcement** — Memories recalled after longer intervals get bigger boosts, cramming produces diminishing returns
- **Cognitive types** — Episodic, semantic, and procedural memories each decay differently, just like in the brain
- **Always-present knowledge** — Pin critical conventions and preferences so they load every session, bypassing recall and never decaying — the facts your agent must never miss
- **Procedural skills** — Reusable how-to workflows with progressive disclosure, learned automatically from repeated experience and exportable to your agent's native skills
- **On-demand depth** — Subcategories are created as needed, not pre-defined
- **Consolidation** — Weak related memories merge into stronger combined knowledge
- **Zero dependencies — and measured, not assumed** — Pure file I/O: no database, no server, no embedding model. That is a deliberate result, not a shortcut. On our hardest retrieval scenario (1,021 memories, 1,000 plausible distractors) a real embedding model ranked the target memories *worse* than BM25 — see the [retrieval-only pilot](benchmark/README.md#retrieval-only-pilot-no-agent-no-llm-spend)

## Install

There are two ways to give an agent its brain. They are complementary — most people end up with both:

| Path | Reaches | Storage | Cost | Best for |
|------|---------|---------|------|----------|
| **Hosted MCP connector** | Every MCP-capable host (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Kilo, Claude.ai apps, ChatGPT, Antigravity, OpenClaw, Hermes, Goose) | Brain Cloud (hosted) | account | One connector, everywhere — including web & mobile chat |
| **Local-first native plugin** | The current CLIs (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Copilot CLI, Kilo, Antigravity) | `~/.brain/` on your machine | free | Zero-config ambient memory, no account, files you own |
| **[Assistant integrations](integrations/)** | OpenClaw / NVIDIA NemoClaw (memory-slot plugin), Hermes Agent (memory provider) | `~/.brain/` on your machine | free | Your always-on personal assistant sharing one brain with your coding agents |
