# GitHub Organization Signal Scanner MCP Server

An MCP server that resolves a company domain to its GitHub organization with repo, language and activity signals. It wraps the Mamba Labs GitHub Organization Signal Scanner actor on Apify and returns a Clay-ready flat JSON row to any MCP client.

## What's Inside

- [What it does](#what-it-does)
- [Quick start](#quick-start)
- [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)
- [Example prompts](#example-prompts)
- [Inputs](#inputs)
- [Output](#output)
- [Example output](#example-output)
- [Features](#features)
- [Full actor documentation](#full-actor-documentation)
- [Mamba Labs GTM Suite](#mamba-labs-gtm-suite)
- [License](#license)

## What it does

Give it a company domain and it finds that company's GitHub organization and returns repository count, followers, creation date, top languages, total stars, the most recent push, how many repositories are actively worked on, and whether the company ships a public SDK. One flat row per company, read through GitHub's own documented REST API.

Forks and archived repositories are excluded from the language and star derivations, and the exclusion is counted on the row. A rate limited request reports `not_extractable` and never a zero, because a zero is a number a buyer would filter on. A login that resolves to a personal user account rather than an organization is reported as `identity_mismatch`. It reads organization and repository metadata only: it does not clone repositories, read source, scan for secrets or assess code quality.

All of the scanning runs on Apify. This package is a thin client that calls the actor and hands back the result unchanged.

## Quick start

You need Node.js 18 or newer and an Apify account with an API token.

Add this to your Claude Desktop config:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mamba-github-organization-signal-scanner": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@mambalabsdev/mcp-github-organization-signal-scanner"],
      "env": {
        "APIFY_TOKEN": "your-apify-token"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Get your token at https://console.apify.com/account/integrations, paste it in, and restart Claude Desktop. The `scan_github_organization_signals` tool will be available.

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 18 or newer
- An Apify account with an API token
- Optional: your own GitHub personal access token, free to create at github.com/settings/tokens with no scopes at all for public data, if you want to scan more than a handful of companies

## Example prompts

- "Find the GitHub organization for stripe.com and summarize its activity."
- "Scan the GitHub org `vercel` and tell me its top languages and total stars."
- "Does figma.com ship a public SDK? Check its GitHub organization."
- "Scan notion.so's GitHub org, counting a repo as active if it was pushed in the last 30 days."

## Inputs

- `company_domain` (optional): bare company domain, for example `stripe.com`. This is the lookup key and the join key for every other actor in the fleet.
- `company_name` (optional but strongly recommended): what the identity gate checks a discovered record against, so supplying it is the cheapest way to reduce wrong matches.
- `github_org` (optional): if you already know the organization login, for example `stripe`, put it here and the tool skips discovery entirely and goes straight to the API, which is faster and spends fewer rate limited requests.
- `includeRepoDetail` (optional): when true (the default) the organization repositories are read and the language, star, activity and SDK signals are derived from them. Set false to return the organization record only, which is one request instead of several and is friendlier to the unauthenticated rate limit.
- `includeContributorEstimate` (optional): when true one extra request reads the contributor count of the organization's most starred repository, as a floor on the size of its public engineering surface. False by default, because one extra request per company is real money against a 60 per hour unauthenticated budget.
- `activeWindowDays` (optional): how recently a repository must have been pushed to count as active. One of `30`, `90`, `180` or `365`, with 90 the default. This changes what active means on the row.
- `repoPageBudget` (optional): how many pages of 100 repositories to read for a large organization. One of `1`, `2`, `3` or `5`. This is a cost and completeness dial, not a change of answer: the row always reports how many repositories were sampled and whether the sample is complete.
- `githubToken` (optional): your own GitHub personal access token, free to create with no scopes at all for public data. Without it the tool runs at GitHub's 60 requests per hour, which is enough for a handful of companies and not enough for a list. With it the limit is 5,000 per hour.
- `skipCache` (optional): when false (the default) a successful lookup is cached for seven days and reused. Set true to force a fresh fetch.
- `max_charge_usd` (optional): a cost cap in USD for this run. The actor stops before an item that could take its charges past this amount. Omit it to rely on the maximum cost per run set in Apify.

## Output

The tool returns the actor's flat JSON row for the company, with 32 snake_case fields and no nested objects. `github_discovery` says how the organization was found, `github_rejected_candidate` records a candidate the identity gate turned away, `repos_sampled` and `repos_complete` say how much of the organization was read, and `repos_excluded` counts the forks and archived repositories left out. See the Apify Store page for the full output schema.

## Example output

{
  "degraded": false,
  "degradation_reason": null,
  "company_domain": "stripe.com",
  "company_name": "Stripe",
  "github_org": "stripe",
  "github_url": "https://github.com/stripe",
  "github_discovery": "homepage_link",
  "github_rejected_candidate": null,
  "github_account_type": "Organization",
  "public_repos": 98,
  "followers": 3469,
  "org_created_at": "2011-0

```bash
# With uvx (no install needed)
uvx mcparmory-github

# With pip
pip install mcparmory-github
mcparmory-github
```

**MCP client configuration** (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Codex, Claude Code):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "github": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["mcparmory-github"],
      "env": {
        "BEARER_TOKEN": "ghp_your_token_here"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Features

Every server in this registry provides:

- **Full API coverage** — all endpoints from the OpenAPI spec are exposed as MCP tools
- **Authentication** — API key, Bearer token, Basic auth, OAuth2, JWT, OpenID Connect, and mutual TLS
- **Multi-auth** — servers that support multiple auth methods let you configure whichever you prefer
- **Pydantic validation** — request parameters are validated before sending to the API
- **Resilience** — configurable retries with exponential backoff, connection pooling, and timeouts
- **Response sanitization** — optional redaction of sensitive fields from API responses

## How servers are generated

Servers are generated by [MCP Blacksmith](https://mcpblacksmith.com), an automated pipeline that:

1. **Parses** an OpenAPI specification
2. **Transforms** operations through LLM-driven passes (naming, parameter filtering, enhancement, classification)
3. **Generates** a complete MCP server with auth, models, validation, and configuration
4. **Tests** every tool against the live API using an autonomous agent
5. **Deploys** passing servers to this registry

The generator targets Python 3.11+ and uses [FastMCP](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) as the MCP framework.

readme.markdown:
# MCP Bundles Hub MCP Server

  

  
  
  
  

> Execute tools from your enabled bundles directly from Claude, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible AI assistants using the Model Context Protocol.

## Download

Download the MCPBundles Hub .mcpb file directly:

**[Download hub.mcpb](https://github.com/thinkchainai/mcpbundles/releases/download/hub-v1.0.0%2Bbuild.8da55d55/hub.mcpb)**

This `.mcpb` package contains a pre-configured MCP server proxy that connects to the MCPBundles Hub endpoint. Once installed, your AI assistant can discover and execute tools from all your enabled bundles.

> **Note**: This repository hosts `.mcpb` files for hundreds of bundles. The link above is specifically for the Hub server. See [all releases](https://github.com/thinkchainai/mcpbundles/releases) to download individual bundle packages.

## What is MCP Bundles?

**MCP Bundles** is the simplest way to connect AI assistants to real-world tools. Instead of configuring hundreds of individual MCP servers, you:

1. **Create bundles** of tools you need (e.g., "Marketing Tools", "Developer Workflow")
2. **Connect providers** with secure OAuth or API keys once
3. **Use one MCP URL** per bundle - all your tools instantly available

With 1,500+ provider integrations including GitHub, Slack, Notion, Google Drive, Salesforce, Stripe, and more, MCP Bundles eliminates the complexity of MCP server management while giving your AI assistant powerful, authenticated access to the services you use every day.

## What is the Hub MCP Server?

The **MCP Bundles Hub MCP Server** provides direct access to tools from all your enabled bundles through a single MCP endpoint. Instead of configuring each bundle separately, you can:

- **Execute Tools**: Run any tool from your enabled bundles through one interface
- **List Available Tools**: Discover what tools are available across all your bundles
- **Search Tools**: Find tools by name, provider, or capability
- **Check Readiness**: Verify bundle configuration and credential status
- **Get Tool Details**: View parameters, descriptions, and usage for specific tools

This server is **authenticated** and tied to your MCPBundles account. It aggregates all your bundle tools into one convenient MCP server endpoint.

## Features

- **OAuth & API Key Authentication**: Secure access via OAuth login or Bearer token  
- **Unified Access**: Execute tools from multiple bundles through one endpoint  
- **Tool Discovery**: Search and list all tools you have access to  
- **Bundle-Aware Execution**: Tools automatically use the correct credentials for each bundle  
- **Readiness Checks**: Verify configuration status before executing tools

## Documentation

For comprehensive setup guides and usage instructions:

- [Model Context Protocol Overview](https://docs.mcpbundles.com/overview/mcp)
- [Setting Up MCP in Cursor](https://docs.mcpbundles.com/how-to/connecting-your-ai#cursor)
- [Setting Up MCP in Claude Desktop](https://docs.mcpbundles.com/how-to/connecting-your-ai#claude-desktop)
- [App-Level Tools Guide](https://docs.mcpbundles.com/how-to/app-level-tools)

## Quick Start

### Prerequisites

- An MCPBundles account (free at [mcpbundles.com](https://mcpbundles.com))
- MCP-compatible client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.)
- Authentication method:
  - **OAuth** (recommended): One-click authentication in Cursor
  - **API Key**: Get from your [dashboard](https://mcpbundles.com/w) for Claude Desktop

### Setup Methods

#### Method 1: One-Click Install in Cursor (Recommended)

Cursor supports direct MCP server installation via URL:

1. Open Cursor Settings → Features → MCP
2. Click **"Add Server"**
3. Paste this URL: `https://github.com/thinkchainai/mcpbundles/releases/download/hub-v1.0.0%2Bbuild.8da55d55/hub.mcpb`
4. Authenticate with OAuth when prompted

#### Method 2: Download & Install .mcpb File

# MCP Bundles Hub MCP Server

  

  
  
  
  

> Execute tools from your enabled bundles directly from Claude, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible AI assistants using the Model Context Protocol.

## Download

Download the MCPBundles Hub .mcpb file directly:

**[Download hub.mcpb](https://github.com/thinkchainai/mcpbundles/releases/download/hub-v1.0.0%2Bbuild.8da55d55/hub.mcpb)**

This `.mcpb` package contains a pre-configured MCP server proxy that connects to the MCPBundles Hub endpoint. Once installed, your AI assistant can discover and execute tools from all your enabled bundles.

> **Note**: This repository hosts `.mcpb` files for hundreds of bundles. The link above is specifically for the Hub server. See [all releases](https://github.com/thinkchainai/mcpbundles/releases) to download individual bundle packages.

## What is MCP Bundles?

**MCP Bundles** is the simplest way to connect AI assistants to real-world tools. Instead of configuring hundreds of individual MCP servers, you:

1. **Create bundles** of tools you need (e.g., "Marketing Tools", "Developer Workflow")
2. **Connect providers** with secure OAuth or API keys once
3. **Use one MCP URL** per bundle - all your tools instantly available

With 1,500+ provider integrations including GitHub, Slack, Notion, Google Drive, Salesforce, Stripe, and more, MCP Bundles eliminates the complexity of MCP server management while giving your AI assistant powerful, authenticated access to the services you use every day.

## What is the Hub MCP Server?

The **MCP Bundles Hub MCP Server** provides direct access to tools from all your enabled bundles through a single MCP endpoint. Instead of configuring each bundle separately, you can:

- **Execute Tools**: Run any tool from your enabled bundles through one interface
- **List Available Tools**: Discover what tools are available across all your bundles
- **Search Tools**: Find tools by name, provider, or capability
- **Check Readiness**: Verify bundle configuration and credential status
- **Get Tool Details**: View parameters, descriptions, and usage for specific tools

This server is **authenticated** and tied to your MCPBundles account. It aggregates all your bundle tools into one convenient MCP server endpoint.

## Features

- **OAuth & API Key Authentication**: Secure access via OAuth login or Bearer token  
- **Unified Access**: Execute tools from multiple bundles through one endpoint  
- **Tool Discovery**: Search and list all tools you have access to  
- **Bundle-Aware Execution**: Tools automatically use the correct credentials for each bundle  
- **Readiness Checks**: Verify configuration status before executing tools

For comprehensive setup guides and usage instructions:

- [Model Context Protocol Overview](https://docs.mcpbundles.com/overview/mcp)

- MCP-compatible client (Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.)
- Authentication method:

4. Authenticate with OAuth when prompted

# 🌟 Microsoft MCP Servers

## 📘 What is MCP?

**Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is an open protocol that standardizes how applications provide context to large language models (LLMs). It allows AI applications to connect with various data sources and tools in a consistent manner, enhancing their capabilities and flexibility. MCP follows a client-server architecture:

- **MCP Hosts**: Applications like AI assistants or IDEs that initiate connections.
- **MCP Clients**: Connectors within the host application that maintain 1:1 connections with servers.
- **MCP Servers**: Services that provide context and capabilities through the standardized MCP.

For more details, visit the [official MCP website](https://modelcontextprotocol.io).

## 📁 Which MCP Servers are built from this repository?

# Playwright Workspaces

> ✅ **Playwright Workspaces is now Generally Available!**

[Playwright Workspaces](https://aka.ms/pww/docs) is a fully managed service for end-to-end web testing, built on top of [Playwright](https://playwright.dev). With Playwright Workspaces, you can significantly speed up test execution by running tests in parallel using managed cloud-based browers. The service takes care of the underlying infrastructure and complexity, allowing you to validate your web app across major browsers on both Linux and Windows—so you can ship features faster and with greater confidence.

👉 [Get started with the Quickstart](https://aka.ms/pww/docs/quickstart)

## Documentation

The full documentation is now available on [**learn.microsoft.com**](https://aka.ms/pww/docs)

There you’ll learn how to:

- Run and scale Playwright tests in the cloud
- Optimize test suite performance and reliability
- Test across multiple browsers and operating systems
- Set up secure, region-aware test environments
- Integrate with CI/CD

## Playwright Cloud Browsers remote MCP (preview)

The [Playwright Cloud Browsers remote MCP server](https://aka.ms/pww/mcp/docs)
gives AI agents managed cloud browsers over Streamable HTTP. Agents can create a
browser session, navigate and inspect pages, interact with elements, and close
the session without installing Playwright or a browser locally.

The remote MCP server is in **preview**, separately from the generally available
Playwright Workspaces service. Preview features do not have a service-level
agreement and are not recommended for production workloads.

### Prerequisites and authentication

You need an Azure subscription, a Playwright workspace with access to the remote
MCP preview, its region and workspace ID, and an identity with permission to use
browser sessions in that workspace.

Use the endpoint for your workspace's region:

```text
https://<region>.mcp.playwright.microsoft.com/playwrightworkspaces/<workspace-id>/mcp
```

Replace both placeholders with your workspace values. Use Microsoft Entra ID
with a client that supports OAuth discovery. The server publishes
protected-resource metadata; your signed-in identity must also have the required
workspace RBAC access. See the [authentication and setup guide](https://aka.ms/pww/mcp/docs)
for permissions and supported compatibility options. Never commit access tokens
or paste them into prompts.

### Connect from VS Code or the GitHub Copilot app

- **VS Code:** Run **MCP: Add Server** from the Command Palette, select **HTTP**,
  enter the resolved workspace endpoint, and choose a configuration destination.
  Follow the server trust and Microsoft Entra sign-in prompts. See
  [Add MCP servers in VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agent-customization/mcp-servers).

name: Holiday Calendar
description: U.S. federal holidays with observed dates and business-day math. Example from an open-source kit.

tools.name: list_federal_holidays
tools.description: List the eleven U.S. federal holidays for one calendar year (2021 through 2100): each holiday's name, its actual date and weekday, the date it is observed when it falls on a weekend (Saturday moves to the Friday before, Sunday to the Monday after), and the rule that sets it, from 5 U.S.C. 6103. Use it to answer which days federal offices close in a year.

inputs.name: year
inputs.description: Calendar year, 2021 through 2100.

tools.name: next_federal_holidays
tools.description: Find the next one to eleven U.S. federal holidays observed on or after a date, with each one's observed date and how many calendar days away it is. Without from_date it starts from today's date in America/New_York and says which date it used.

inputs.name: from_date
inputs.description: Start looking on this date, inclusive, written YYYY-MM-DD (for example 2026-11-26). Covers 2021 through 2100.

inputs.name: count
inputs.description: How many upcoming holidays to return, 1 to 11. Defaults to 1.

tools.name: check_business_day
tools.description: Check whether a date is a U.S. business day (a weekday that is not an observed federal holiday). Returns the weekday, the holiday observed that day if any, and the business days just before and just after it.

inputs.name: date
inputs.description: The date to check, written YYYY-MM-DD (for example 2026-11-26). Covers 2021 through 2100.

tools.name: add_business_days
tools.description: Move a number of U.S. business days forward or backward from a date, skipping weekends and observed federal holidays, for due dates, delivery windows and notice periods. The start date is not counted: 1 business day after a Friday is the next Monday, or Tuesday when that Monday is a holiday. Returns the resulting date and every holiday it skipped. Up to 1,000 business days either way.

inputs.name: start_date
inputs.description: The date to count from. It is not counted itself, written YYYY-MM-DD (for example 2026-11-26). Covers 2021 through 2100.

inputs.name: business_days
inputs.description: Business days to move, -1000 to 1000. Negative counts backward. 0 returns the start date if it is a business day, otherwise the next one.

tools.name: count_business_days
tools.description: Count the U.S. business days between two dates, both dates included, leaving out weekends and observed federal holidays. Returns the business day count, the weekend days, and each holiday that fell in the span. Spans up to 3,660 calendar days.

inputs.name: start_date
inputs.description: First date of the span, counted if it is a business day, written YYYY-MM-DD (for example 2026-11-26). Covers 2021 through 2100.

inputs.name: end_date
inputs.description: Last date of the span, counted if it is a business day, written YYYY-MM-DD (for example 2026-11-26). Covers 2021 through 2100.

# Small Business MCP Starter Kit by Modern Mustard Seed

Ship a remote MCP connector for Claude that is built to pass Anthropic's directory review on the first try.

This kit is the set of patterns Modern Mustard Seed uses for the connectors it runs in production, pulled out into a clean Next.js project you can fork:

- **A route template** on Next.js App Router and [`mcp-handler`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-handler), serving Streamable HTTP at one URL per connector, with no redirect.
- **Tool conventions enforced at load time**: a title, `readOnlyHint` or `destructiveHint` on every tool, snake_case names of 64 characters or fewer, and descriptions that describe instead of steer. Break a rule and `pnpm test` fails, long before a reviewer sees it.
- **Specific error messages** instead of "Bad Request", and **output size caps** under Claude's limits.
- **Rate limiting built for Claude's shared egress range.** Every claude.ai user arrives from `160.79.104.0/21`, so nothing is keyed by IP and nothing returns HTTP 429.
- **An SSRF-safe fetch** for any tool that reads a URL a user supplied, with tests that prove a listening loopback server receives zero requests.
- **An eval harness** that runs real prompts against your live URL, with no model and no API key.
- **Docs, privacy, terms and support page templates** plus `/.well-known/security.txt`, all driven by one config file.
- **A submission checklist** mapped to the directory form's 10 steps and its seven policy acknowledgments, with every rule linked to Anthropic's documentation.
- **A worked example**: a U.S. federal holiday and business-day calendar with five read-only tools that passes all 35 of its own evals.

MIT licensed. Built by [Modern Mustard Seed](https://modernmustardseed.com).

## Working demo

The example connector runs live, deployed from this repository with no changes:

- Connector URL: `https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/holidays` (add it in Claude under **Customize > Connectors > Add custom connector**)
- Docs page reviewers read: https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/docs/holidays
- Privacy, terms and support: https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/privacy, [/terms](https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/terms), [/support](https://starter.modernmustardseed.com/support)
- Official MCP Registry entry: `com.modernmustardseed/holiday-calendar`

Run the evals against it yourself: `node eval/holidays.eval.mjs https://starter.modernmustardseed.com`

## Quickstart: 10 minutes

You need Node 22.6 or later, pnpm, and a Vercel account (any host that runs Next.js works).

**1. Make your copy.** (1 minute)

```sh
gh repo create my-connector --template ModernMustardSeed/small-business-mcp-starter --public --clone
cd my-connector
pnpm install
```

Or select **Use this template** on GitHub.

**2. Run it and prove it works.** (2 minutes)

```sh
pnpm dev
```

In a second terminal:

```sh
pnpm test
pnpm evals http://localhost:3000
```

You should see `32 pass` from the unit tests and `35 of 35 passed` from the evals. Open http://localhost:3000/docs/holidays to see the docs page reviewers read.

**3. Make it yours.** (2 minutes)

Edit `lib/site.ts`: company name, location, website, support inbox, security inbox, and the policy date. Every public page and `security.txt` read from it. Replace `app/icon.svg` and `app/apple-icon.png` with your own mark; the directory listing asks for an icon.

**4. Deploy.** (3 minutes)

Import the repository at [vercel.com/new](https://vercel.com/new), or from the terminal:

```sh
vercel deploy --prod
```

Vercel sets `VERCEL_PROJECT_PRODUCTION_URL`, which the pages use for their links. Leave Attack Challenge Mode and any bot-protection rule off for your MCP paths: they answer Claude with a challenge page.

**5. Check the deployment.** (1 minute)

```sh
pnpm preflight https://your-project.vercel.app
pnpm evals https://your-project.vercel.app
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli https://your-project.vercel.app/holidays --transport http --method tools/list
```

Preflight checks HTTPS, no redirect, no 403 or 429, every public page returning 200, the MCP handshake and the annotation rules.

**6. Try it in Claude.** (1 minute)

In Claude, open **Customize > Connectors > Add custom connector** and paste `https://your-project.vercel.app/holidays`. Ask: "An invoice dated 2026-11-20 is due in 10 business days. What date is that?" In Claude Code:

```sh
claude mcp add --transport http holidays https://your-project.vercel.app/holidays
```

## Build your own connector

1. Copy `lib/holidays/tools.ts` to `lib/<yours>/tools.ts`. Declare each tool as a `ToolSpec`: name, title, description, zod input schema, annotations, a per-minute limit, optional global limits, the fields that are safe to log, and a `run` function that returns `ok(data)` or `fail(code, sentence)`.
2. Copy `app/holidays/route.ts` to `app/<yours>/route.ts` and point it at your tools.
3. Copy `app/docs/holidays/page.tsx` to `app/docs/<yours>/page.tsx`. Keep the "For reviewers" section: you paste it into the form.
4. Rewrite `app/privacy/page.tsx` so every sentence is true of your tools: what they receive, what they read, what you keep and for how long, who else touches it.
5. Copy `eval/holidays.eval.mjs`. Write 20 to 50 cases from prompts real users type, with expected values from an authority outside your code. Include the error cases.
6. If a tool fetches a URL a user gave you, use `safeFetch` from `lib/mcp/safe-fetch.ts`. Never `fetch` a user-supplied URL directly.
7. Deploy, run `pnpm preflight` and `pnpm evals` against production, test every tool in Claude, then work through [docs/SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md](docs/SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md).

Why each pattern exists, with the rule it answers: [docs/PATTERNS.md](docs/PATTERNS.md).

## What is in the box

| Path | What it does |
|---|---|
| `app/holidays/route.ts` | The connector endpoint. One file per connector. |
| `lib/mcp/tool.ts` | `ToolSpec`, `registerTools`, `runTool`: conventions, limits, e

…

name: Mode VC Chart: Vercel AI SDK Downloads vs. the Lab SDKs
description: The Vercel AI SDK fell from 31 to 23 weekly downloads per 100 downloads of the OpenAI,.

tools.name: get_distribution_moat_score
tools.description: Rule-based 1 to 5 score of distribution defensibility, using only the acquisition channels you list and whether you have proprietary data or network effects. business_model is echoed back and does not change the score. It is a discussion aid built from Mode VC's published thesis, not a valuation, not an investment decision and not a prediction.

inputs.name: product_name
inputs.description: Name of the startup or product

inputs.name: business_model
inputs.description: Primary business model (echoed, not scored)

inputs.name: acquisition_channels
inputs.description: Key distribution channels. Channels containing hardware_bundle, network_lockin, viral_loop, system_default or native_integration raise the score.

inputs.name: has_proprietary_data_or_network
inputs.description: Does user activity generate compounding data or network lock-in?

tools.name: get_venture_chart_of_the_day
tools.description: Returns the most recent charts from Mode VC's Chart of the Day archive (one new chart per day, mostly AI model, adoption, developer-package and pricing data), newest first, each with its claim, takeaway, URL and cited sources.

inputs.name: limit
inputs.description: Number of recent charts. Default 3.

tools.name: search_charts
tools.description: Searches every chart in the Mode VC Chart of the Day archive by keyword over title, claim, takeaway and keywords. Returns claims, takeaways, canonical URLs, markdown endpoints and cited sources. The archive grows by one chart a day; the response states its current size.

inputs.name: query
inputs.description: Search term, e.g. "pricing", "claude", "inference", "sdk"

inputs.name: limit
inputs.description: Maximum charts to return. Default 10.

tools.name: get_chart_data
tools.description: Returns one chart from the Chart of the Day archive: the data table behind it (rows as published), claim, takeaway, note and the sources it cites. Look up by slug or title. Data is as published on the chart page; follow source_urls for the original data.

inputs.name: slug
inputs.description: Chart slug or title, e.g. "pre-seed-valuation-dispersion", "ai-inference-cost-comparison"

tools.name: search_investors
tools.description: Searches the Mode VC Investor Atlas, a directory of venture capital firms and their partners compiled from public information (counts are in the response). Filter by firm or partner name, sector, entry stage, and headquarters or location. Stage and check size are as reported by each firm where available; it does not hold portfolio companies or fund performance.

inputs.name: query
inputs.description: Firm or partner name, e.g. "a16z", "Benchmark", "Marc Andreessen", "Khosla"

inputs.name: sector
inputs.description: Sector slug, e.g. "ai-and-data", "dev-tools-and-infra", "enterprise-software", "fintech", "crypto", "healthtech", "climate", "consumer"

inputs.name: stage
inputs.description: Entry stage the firm reports investing at

inputs.name: location
inputs.description: Geographic hub, e.g. "california", "new-york", "massachusetts", "toronto", "united-states"

inputs.name: limit
inputs.description: Maximum firms to return. Default 10.

tools.name: get_investor_details
tools.description: Returns one firm from the Investor Atlas: headquarters and locations, website and social links, latest fund as listed, reported entry stages, check size bands (lowest and highest the firm reports) and lead preference where known, sectors, and up to 12 partner names (the total partner count is also given). It does not include portfolio companies or investment theses.

inputs.name: slug_or_name
inputs.description: Firm slug or name, e.g. "andreessen-horowitz", "sequoia-capital", "accel", "406-ventures"

tools.name: get_mode_vc_thesis_and_criteria
tools.description: Returns Mode VC's published investment parameters as stated on https://modevc.com/thesis: ticket size, geography focus, stage, core conviction and how to pitch.

tools.name: calc_safe_dilution
tools.description: Models how stacked SAFEs convert at a priced round and what the founders keep, including the option pool top-up (pool in the pre-money or post-money). Same math as https://modevc.com/tools/safe-calculator. Illustrative model, not legal or tax advice.

inputs.name: initial_shares
inputs.description: Fully diluted shares before the SAFEs convert. Web default 10,000,000.

inputs.name: existing_pool_pct
inputs.description: Option pool already inside the initial shares, in percent. Web default 5.

inputs.name: founder_split_pct
inputs.description: Your share of the founder block, in percent. Web default 50.

inputs.name: priced_pre_money
inputs.description: Priced round pre-money valuation in USD. Web default 16,000,000.

inputs.name: priced_investment
inputs.description: New money in the priced round in USD. Web default 4,000,000.

inputs.name: target_pool_pct
inputs.description: Option pool size after the round, in percent. Web default 10.

inputs.name: pool_mode
inputs.description: pre_money: the pool top-up dilutes founders and SAFEs only. post_money: everyone is diluted. Web default pre_money.

inputs.name: safes
inputs.description: The SAFEs to convert. Omit to use the web calculator example of two SAFEs.

tools.name: calc_83b_qsbs_delaware
tools.description: Computes the 83(b) filing deadline and tax on the grant, the federal tax saved by a QSBS (Section 1202) exclusion at a given sale price, and Delaware franchise tax under both methods. Federal tax only, top federal rates assumed, no state tax or AMT. Same math as https://modevc.com/tools/83b-qsbs-calculator. Illustrative model, not tax advice.

inputs.name: grant_date
inputs.description: Date the shares were transferred, YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to today.

inputs.name: issue_date
inputs.description: QSBS stock issue date, YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to the grant date. Stock issued after 2025-07-04 gets the 50/75/100 percent steps at 3/4/5 years.

inputs.name: as_of_date
inputs.description: Date used for the days-to-deadline count. Defaults to today (UTC).

inputs.name: shares_granted
inputs.description: Web default 4,000,000.

readme.markdown:
# MSG91 MCP

Lets AI assistants work with [MSG91](https://msg91.com): find the right MSG91 API for SMS, OTP, WhatsApp, Email, Voice and more, read its parameters, and call it correctly.

This is a remote MCP server (Streamable HTTP) at `https://mcp.msg91.com/mcp`. Nothing to install and no API key for the server itself.

## Tools
| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `search_msg91_docs` | Search the MSG91 documentation with a natural-language question |
| `get_msg91_api_docs` | Browse the MSG91 API docs module by module, down to one endpoint as an OpenAPI file |
| `quickstart-msg91` | How to run any MSG91 API from the terminal |

## Connect from Cline
Install it from the Cline MCP Marketplace, or open **MCP Servers → Configure MCP Servers** and add this to `cline_mcp_settings.json`:
```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "msg91": {
      "type": "streamableHttp",
      "url": "https://mcp.msg91.com/mcp",
      "disabled": false,
      "autoApprove": []
    }
  }
}
```
Agent-driven install steps are in [llms-install.md](llms-install.md).

## Connect from Claude Code
```bash
claude mcp add --transport http msg91 https://mcp.msg91.com/mcp
```

## Calling the MSG91 API
Run any MSG91 endpoint from your terminal (Node.js 18+):
```bash
npx docstar-cli msg91 <module> <endpoint> --<flag> "<value>"
# e.g.
npx docstar-cli msg91 whatsapp send-message-in-text --integrated_number "91XXXXXXXXXX" \
  --recipient_number "91YYYYYYYYYY" --content_type "text" --text "Hello"
```
The CLI asks for your MSG91 authkey in the terminal and can save it. Do not paste your authkey into an AI chat.

## MCP Registry
[server.json](server.json) is the listing for the official MCP Registry, as `com.msg91/mcp`. The `com.msg91` name is proven by owning the `msg91.com` domain.

One-time setup: create a signing key and publish its public half on `msg91.com` (Git Bash or any shell with OpenSSL):
```bash
openssl genpkey -algorithm Ed25519 -out mcp-registry-key.pem
echo "v=MCPv1; k=ed25519; p=$(openssl pkey -in mcp-registry-key.pem -pubout -outform DER | tail -c 32 | base64)"
```
Add the printed line as a TXT record on `msg91.com`. Keep `mcp-registry-key.pem` private and out of this repo.

Publish (bump `version` first for any later change):
```bash
mcp-publisher login dns --domain msg91.com --private-key "$(openssl pkey -in mcp-registry-key.pem -noout -text | grep -A3 'priv:' | tail -n +2 | tr -d ' :\n')"
mcp-publisher publish
```

## Links
- Website: https://msg91.com

# Murphy's Laws

A comprehensive collection of Murphy's Laws - humorous observations about life's tendency for things to go wrong.

Available on the **Web**, with iOS and Android releases forthcoming.

## Platforms

- **Web**: <https://murphys-laws.com> (PWA - installable, works offline)
- **iOS**: Coming Soon
- **Android**: Coming Soon

## AI & Developer Integration

Four official ways to integrate Murphy's Laws. No API key for reads.

| Package | npm | Purpose |
|---------|-----|---------|
| [`murphys-laws-sdk`](sdk/) | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/murphys-laws-sdk.svg?label=)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-sdk) | Typed TypeScript client, zero deps |
| [`murphys-laws-cli`](cli/) | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/murphys-laws-cli.svg?label=)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-cli) | Command-line interface (`npx murphys-laws-cli`) |
| [`murphys-laws-mcp`](mcp/) | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/murphys-laws-mcp.svg?label=)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-mcp) | Model Context Protocol server for AI agents |
| [REST API](shared/docs/API.md) | - | Public HTTP API at `https://murphys-laws.com/api/v1/` |

Full details and examples on the [developer landing page](https://murphys-laws.com/developers).

### REST API

Public API at `https://murphys-laws.com/api/v1/`, no auth required for reads.

- [API Documentation](shared/docs/API.md)
- [OpenAPI spec](https://murphys-laws.com/openapi.json)
- [llms.txt](https://murphys-laws.com/llms.txt) | [llms-full.txt](https://murphys-laws.com/llms-full.txt)

### TypeScript SDK

[`murphys-laws-sdk`](sdk/) on [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-sdk) is a tiny typed client over the REST API with zero runtime dependencies.

```ts
import { MurphysLawsClient } from 'murphys-laws-sdk';
const law = await new MurphysLawsClient().getRandomLaw();
```

### Command-line interface

[`murphys-laws-cli`](cli/) on [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-cli) wraps the API for scripts and terminal use.

```bash
npx murphys-laws-cli random
npx murphys-laws-cli search "computer" --limit 3
```

### MCP Server (Model Context Protocol)

An [MCP server](mcp/) lets AI agents (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code Copilot) query Murphy's Laws directly.

Quick start, no clone needed:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "murphys-laws": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "murphys-laws-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

7 tools: `search_laws`, `get_random_law`, `get_law_of_the_day`, `get_law`, `list_categories`, `get_laws_by_category`, `submit_law`.

See [mcp/README.md](mcp/README.md) or [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/murphys-laws-mcp), or the [developer landing page](https://murphys-laws.com/developers) for the full picture.

## Repository Structure

This is a monorepo containing:

```
murphys-laws/
├── backend/        # Node.js API server (TypeScript runtime via tsx)
├── web/            # Web application (TypeScript + Vite)
├── mcp/            # MCP server for AI agent integration (npm: murphys-laws-mcp)
├── sdk/            # TypeScript SDK over the public REST API (npm: murphys-laws-sdk)
├── cli/            # Command-line interface (npm: murphys-laws-cli)
├── ios/            # iOS app (Swift + SwiftUI)
├── android/        # Android app (Kotlin + Jetpack Compose)
└── shared/         # Shared resources and documentation
```

## Quick Start

### Backend (API Server)

```bash
cd backend
npm install
npm run build:db # Build SQLite database
npm run dev # Start API server
npm start # Run API from src/server/api-server.ts via tsx
```

### Web Application

```bash
cd web
npm install
npm run dev # Start dev server
```

### iOS App

```bash
cd ios
open MurphysLaws.xcodeproj
# Press ⌘R to run
```

### Android App

```bash
cd android
./gradlew assembleDebug
# Or open in Android Studio
```

## Documentation

- **Architecture**: [Mobile Architecture Guide](shared/docs/MOBILE-ARCHITECTURE.md)
- **MCP Server**: [MCP README](mcp/README.md)
- **API**: [API Documentation](shared/docs/API.md)
- **iOS**: [iOS PRD](shared/docs/MOBILE-IOS-PRD.md)
- **Android**: [Android PRD](shared/docs/MOBILE-ANDROID-PRD.md)
- **Deployment**: [Deployment Guide](shared/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md)
- **Repository Structure**: [Repository Structure Guide](shared/docs/MOBILE-REPOSITORY-STRUCTURE.md)

## Testing

```bash

# Test a subset only

npm run test:web       # Web Vitest suite only (no E2E)

```

## Development

### Prerequisites

- Node.js 22+
- For iOS: macOS, Xcode 15+
- For Android: Android Studio Hedgehog+, JDK 17+

### Install Dependencies

```bash
# Install all dependencies (root and workspaces)
npm run install:all

# Or install individually
cd backend && npm install
cd web && npm install
```

### Run Development Servers

```bash
# Run backend + web concurrently

# Or run individually

```

**Note**: The `predev` script automatically cleans up any orphaned processes using ports 8787 and 5175 before starting.

### Troubleshooting Port Issues

If you encounter `EADDRINUSE` errors (port already in use):

```bash

# Automatically kill processes using development ports
```

# Neon MCP Server

**Neon MCP Server** is an open-source tool that lets you interact with your Lakebase Postgres databases on Neon in **natural language**.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a [standardized protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) designed to manage context between large language models (LLMs) and external systems. This repository provides a remote MCP Server for [Neon](https://neon.com).

Neon's MCP server acts as a bridge between natural language requests and the [Neon API](https://neon.com/docs/reference/api). Built upon MCP, it translates your requests into the necessary API calls, enabling you to manage tasks such as creating projects and branches, running queries, and performing database migrations seamlessly.

Some of the key features of the Neon MCP server include:

- **Natural language interaction:** Manage Neon databases using intuitive, conversational commands.
- **Simplified database management:** Perform complex actions without writing SQL or directly using the Neon API.
- **Accessibility for non-developers:** Empower users with varying technical backgrounds to interact with Neon databases.
- **Database migration support:** Leverage Neon's branching capabilities for database schema changes initiated via natural language.

For example, in Claude Code, or any MCP Client, you can use natural language to accomplish things with Neon, such as:

- `Let's create a new Postgres database, and call it "my-database". Let's then create a table called users with the following columns: id, name, email, and password.`
- `I want to run a migration on my project called "my-project" that alters the users table to add a new column called "created_at".`
- `Can you give me a summary of all of my Neon projects and what data is in each one?`

> [!WARNING]  
> **Neon MCP Server Security Considerations**  
> The Neon MCP Server grants powerful database management capabilities through natural language requests. **Always review and authorize actions requested by the LLM before execution.** Ensure that only authorized users and applications have access to the Neon MCP Server.
>
> The Neon MCP Server is intended for local development and IDE integrations only. **We do not recommend using the Neon MCP Server in production environments.** It can execute powerful operations that may lead to accidental or unauthorized changes.
>
> For more information, see [MCP security guidance →](https://neon.com/docs/ai/neon-mcp-server#mcp-security-guidance).

## Setting up Neon MCP Server

There are a few options for setting up the Neon MCP Server:

1. **Quick Setup with API Key (Cursor, VS Code, and Claude Code):** Run [`neon@latest init`](https://neon.com/docs/cli/init) to automatically configure Neon's MCP Server, [agent skills](https://github.com/neondatabase/agent-skills), and VS Code extension with one command.
2. **Remote MCP Server (OAuth Based Authentication):** Connect to Neon's managed MCP server using OAuth for authentication. This method is more convenient as it eliminates the need to manage API keys. Additionally, you will automatically receive the latest features and improvements as soon as they are released.
3. **Remote MCP Server (API Key Based Authentication):** Connect to Neon's managed MCP server using API key for authentication. This method is useful if you want to connect a remote agent to Neon where OAuth is not available. Additionally, you will automatically receive the latest features and improvements as soon as they are released.

### Prerequisites

- An MCP Client application.
- A [Neon account](https://console.neon.tech/signup).
- **Node.js (>= v18.0.0):** Download from [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org).
- If [IP Allow](https://neon.com/docs/introduction/ip-allow) is enabled, add `34.192.103.46` and `23.22.233.166` to your allowlist (`mcp.neon.tech` static IPs).

For development, you'll need Node.js 22+ (pnpm is provided via Corepack — run `corepack enable` to activate it).

### Option 1. Quick Setup with API Key

**Don't want to manually create an API key?**

Run [`neon@latest init`](https://neon.com/docs/cli/init) to automatically configure Neon's MCP Server with one command:

```bash
npx neon@latest init
```

This works with Cursor, VS Code (GitHub Copilot), and Claude Code. It will authenticate via OAuth, create a Neon API key for you, and configure your editor automatically.

### Option 2. Remote Hosted MCP Server (OAuth Based Authentication)

Connect to Neon's managed MCP server using OAuth for authentication. This is the easiest setup, requires no local installation of this server, and doesn't need a Neon API key configured in the client.

Run the following command to add the Neon MCP Server for all detected agents and editors in your workspace:

```bash
npx add-mcp "https://mcp.neon.tech/mcp?category=projects&category=branches&category=endpoints&category=querying&category=schema"
```

That URL publishes projects, branches, compute endpoints, querying, and schema. Preview it with `/api/list-tools?category=projects&category=branches&category=endpoints&category=querying&category=schema`. The unfiltered URL publishes every category:

```bash
npx add-mcp https://mcp.neon.tech/mcp
```

Add the `-g` flag to add the Neon MCP Server to the global MCP server list instead of project-scoped.

Alternatively, you can add the following "Neon" entry to your client's MCP server configuration file (e.g., `mcp.json`, `mcp_config.json`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "Neon": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://mcp.neon.tech/mcp?category=projects&category=branches&category=endpoints&category=querying&category=schema"
    }
  }
}
```

**Kiro:** Add the following to your Kiro MCP config file (`~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json` for global, or `.kiro/settings/mcp.json` for project-scoped):

readme.markdown:
# NexaTabs

NexaTabs is a free browser extension for Chrome and Edge that organizes your tabs into named workspaces. Save a full set of tabs, switch between projects in one click, and pick up where you left off. It is local-first and privacy-first: your workspaces, notes and settings are stored in your browser, and no NexaTabs account is needed for the core features.

By Nebula Personalization Tech Solutions Pvt. Ltd.

## Install

- [NexaTabs on the Chrome Web Store](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/nexatabs/ndehmhgkmhhkcopmajkpknnhhbcdpcmo)
- [NexaTabs on Microsoft Edge Add-ons](https://microsoftedge.microsoft.com/addons/detail/nexatabs/jckmengicgkfojgcgipimfilkjelndlc)
- Website: [www.nexatabs.com](https://www.nexatabs.com)

NexaTabs supports Chrome and Edge. Both use the same NexaTabs build. NexaTabs is free forever in its present form.

## Key features

- **Workspaces:** Save a full set of tabs as a named workspace and switch projects in one click or with Alt+Q, without rebuilding your session. Switching restores saved URLs; unsaved in-page form data is not kept.
- **Save and Close:** Save a workspace's open tabs and close them in one action. Stash moves loose tabs (not grouped, not pinned) into a workspace; it asks first and closes only what it saved.
- **Accounts (same site · multiple logins, experimental):** Separate cookie jars let you stay signed in to more than one account on the same site in one browser. Accounts is experimental: site support varies, some sites may block or detect multiple logins, and it is not a replacement for separate operating system profiles when you need hard separation.
- **Notes and Quick Note:** Plain-text notes for each workspace, plus a floating Quick Note for prompts and reminders.
- **Workspace Bookmarks:** Keep a per-workspace list of reference links without keeping those tabs open.
- **Import Wizard (beta):** Bring in Chrome tab groups, browser bookmarks, URL lists, or exports from other tab tools. It adds to what you have and does not replace your existing workspaces.
- **Duplicate, export and import a workspace:** Duplicate a workspace in one click, or export one workspace as a JSON file and import it back as a new copy. Import never overwrites an existing workspace.
- **Local JSON backup:** Export all workspaces and settings as a local JSON file. Import backup replaces all NexaTabs data, and only after you confirm.
- **Open alongside:** Open a saved workspace next to what is already open, without clearing the current window.
- **Pin and protect:** Pin key workspaces and turn on protection so they are harder to rename or delete by accident.
- **Auto-organize:** Optional suggestions that group open tabs into workspaces such as AI, work, personal or lifestyle. Suggestions are optional and may not match every browsing pattern.
- **Context menus:** Right-click a page or the toolbar icon and choose Save page to NexaTabs workspace (the page stays open), or right-click a link and choose Bookmark link to workspace.
- **Add URLs by paste:** Paste a list of links into a workspace; duplicates are skipped.
- **Zen Mode:** A calmer dashboard of glass workspace cards over an optional scenic or custom wallpaper. The cards adjust to light or dark photos, and you can click a card to open its workspace. It changes the look only; your workspaces stay as they are.
- **Accessibility:** Keyboard-friendly flows, larger click targets, and support for your system's reduced-motion and contrast settings.
- **Languages:** English, French, German and Spanish (Latin America).

For full details and limits, see the [Features page](https://www.nexatabs.com/features) and the [Answers hub](https://www.nexatabs.com/answers).

## Privacy and permissions

NexaTabs stores your workspace data locally in your browser. There is no NexaTabs account and no cloud sync. See [PRIVACY.md](PRIVACY.md) for a plain-language explanation of each browser permission and of how website icons are loaded, and the full [NexaTabs Privacy Policy](https://www.nexatabs.com/privacy-policy).

## Changelog

See [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) for what changed in each release.

## Support

For how-tos and common questions, see the [NexaTabs Answers hub](https://www.nexatabs.com/answers) and the [NexaTabs Support page](https://www.nexatabs.com/support).

For help or bug reports, email support@nebulatech.in. Please include your browser (Chrome or Edge), the NexaTabs version, what happened, and the steps to reproduce it.

## About this repository

This repository holds public documentation for NexaTabs: this README, the permissions and privacy explainer, and the changelog. The NexaTabs source code is not public and is not included here. The extension is distributed only through the Chrome Web Store and Microsoft Edge Add-ons.

NexaTabs is developed and maintained by Nebula Personalization Tech Solutions Pvt. Ltd. ([www.nebulatech.in](https://www.nebulatech.in))

# nlqdb — your autonomous DBA.

> nlqdb attaches to the Postgres or Cloudflare D1 database you already run, proposes the changes it needs, applies the ones you approve, measures them, and reverts any that regress.

Why it exists: [the mission](docs/END_GOAL.md#mission) — encapsulate the trial-and-error journey every company walks to a good database infrastructure.

Where it is going ([`docs/END_GOAL.md`](docs/END_GOAL.md)): paste a
connection string — on nlqdb.com, with the CLI, through the SDK, or from your
coding agent over MCP — and the first proposals arrive within minutes, each
with its expected effect, cost and inverse. Apply is one click; nlqdb then
measures p95 on the same queries and keeps the change or reverts it, never on
your app's request path. That loop is being built
([Roadmap](#roadmap)); what is live today is the hosted product below.

**No backend to build.** You write HTML; each
component asks for what it wants in plain English; nlqdb infers the schema,
writes the SQL, runs it, and renders the result. There is no backend for you
to build.

Two actions. That's the whole product:

1. **Create a database** — one word: a name (or a goal).
2. **Talk to it** in plain English.

```html
<script src="https://elements.nlqdb.com/v1.js" type="module"></script>

<nlq-data
  goal="the 5 newest orders, with customer and item"
  api-key="pk_live_xxx"
  template="table"
  refresh="10s"
></nlq-data>
```

That's the entire backend for a live order list — no API to write, no
schema to define, no JSON to parse. Engine choice (Postgres / Mongo /
Redis / DuckDB / pgvector / …), schema inference, indexing, backups, and
auto-migration between engines based on your real workload are background
concerns you never have to see.

## Status — early, open

nlqdb is **early** and built in the open, but fully public — no gate, no
invite code. The marketing site, the `/v1/ask` pipeline, the `<nlq-data>` /
`<nlq-action>` elements, the chat app, the TypeScript SDK, the hosted MCP
server, and the `nlq` CLI are all live in some form (see the surface table
below). Natural-language → SQL accuracy is still climbing toward our public
bar (BIRD ≥ 0.65, Spider 2.0 ≥ 0.75 on the free model chain), so answers can
be wrong — every response carries a confidence signal and the SQL it ran.

## Use it

Connecting an agent over MCP? On **Claude Code**, one marketplace add wires the
hosted server *and* both memory skills in a single step:

```
/plugin marketplace add nlqdb/nlqdb
/plugin install nlqdb-memory@nlqdb
```

On any other MCP host, [**connect your agent**](https://docs.nlqdb.com/agent-memory/)
with one browser-OAuth approval; headless hosts skip the browser with
`npx -y @nlqdb/mcp` and an `sk_mcp_*` MCP key
([MCP setup](https://docs.nlqdb.com/mcp/)). `@nlqdb/sdk` and `@nlqdb/mcp`
are both published and importable from npm.

The 60-second walkthrough — plain HTML, CLI, and ten framework wrappers —
lives at [`docs.nlqdb.com`](https://docs.nlqdb.com). Start with the
[HTML tutorial](https://docs.nlqdb.com/tutorials/html/) or the
[CLI tutorial](https://docs.nlqdb.com/tutorials/cli/).

You don't generate an API key separately: describe your database at
[nlqdb.com](https://nlqdb.com/?utm_source=github), and the chat hands you a
`<nlq-data>` snippet with the key already inlined.

## Examples

[`examples/`](./examples) — minimal scaffolds in plain HTML, Next.js,
Nuxt, SvelteKit, Astro, plus a CLI-only walkthrough. Each is the smallest
valid integration around one `<nlq-data>` element or one CLI session.

## What makes it different

Four things every release has to move, none allowed to regress
([`GLOBAL-025`](./docs/decisions/GLOBAL-025-north-star.md)):

- **Engine quality** — natural-language → SQL accuracy (measured
  continuously on BIRD + Spider 2.0 + an internal eval), plus the
  multi-engine layer that moves your data to the right engine for your
  workload.
- **Onboarding** — landing to first answer in under a minute, no card,
  no config.
- **UX** — see the diff before any write, see the SQL behind every
  answer, and on low confidence get a one-click clarify — a guided turn,
  never a dead-end, and never a silent guess.
- **Performance** — sub-400 ms cached, sub-1.5 s cold.

The bet: get this right on free, open models and it only gets better on
frontier ones — the scaffolding compounds with whatever model is
underneath.

## Models & plans

- **Free forever** on the built-in open-model chain — queries, embeds,
  and the elements, no card required.
- **Bring your own LLM key** (Anthropic / OpenAI / Gemini / Grok / OpenRouter)
  on any tier, at no markup.
- **Hosted premium models** on paid plans, when you'd rather not manage a
  key of your own.
- **Self-host the source** — the engine, CLI, MCP server, and SDKs are
  source-available under [FSL-1.1-ALv2](./LICENSE): free to self-host for
  any non-competing use, bring your own LLM key, no per-call fees. The
  license auto-converts to Apache 2.0 two years after each release.

The hosted-premium model lane went live 2026-08-14. The full model strategy is in
[`GLOBAL-026`](./docs/decisions/GLOBAL-026-llm-strategy-byollm-hosted-premium.md).

## Surfaces at a glance

| Surface | Status | Where |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP API (`POST /v1/ask`, `POST /v1/run`, `POST /v1/insert`) | ✓ shipped | `apps/api/src/ask/**` |
| `<nlq-data>` + `<nlq-action>` elements | ✓ shipped (v0.1) | `packages/elements/**` |
| `@nlqdb/sdk` (TypeScript) | ✓ shipped (incl. `runSql` + cross-tenant grant + pack-import runner verbs) — installable from npm; `insert()` and `runSql` `params` publish in `0.5.0` | `packages/sdk/**` |
| Framework wrappers (React / Next / Vue / Nuxt / Svelte / SvelteKit / Astro / Solid + Swift) | ~ built + CI-tested; npm / SPM publish pending | `packages/{react,next,…}/**` |
| Chat app `nlqdb.com/app` | ✓ shipped | `apps/web/**` |
| Hosted MCP server `mcp.nlqdb.com/mcp` | ✓ shipped (host auto-detect pending) | `apps/mcp/**`, `packages/mcp/**` |
| Local stdio MCP server `@nlqdb/m

OneUptime is an open-source observability platform. It checks that your websites, APIs and servers work, collects the logs, metrics and traces your apps send, pages whoever is on call when something breaks, and tells your customers on a status page. It all happens in one product, so the tool that notices a problem is the one that pages your team.

You can use it on [OneUptime Cloud](https://oneuptime.com) or run it on your own servers.

  

## What it does

- **[Monitoring](https://oneuptime.com/docs/monitor/create-monitor)**: Check websites, APIs, ports, DNS and certificates from probes around the world or from inside your own network. OneUptime also watches servers, Kubernetes, Docker, VMware, databases and network devices.
- **[Incidents and on-call](https://oneuptime.com/docs/incidents/index)**: Work each incident on one timeline. Page whoever is on call by phone, SMS, email, push, Slack or Microsoft Teams, and escalate until someone responds.
- **[Status pages](https://oneuptime.com/docs/status-pages/index)**: Keep customers informed on public or private status pages, and announce scheduled maintenance there.
- **[Logs, metrics and traces](https://oneuptime.com/docs/telemetry/open-telemetry)**: Send them with OpenTelemetry, search them and build dashboards. Exceptions, profiles, real user monitoring and security events live in the same place.
- **[Workflows and runbooks](https://oneuptime.com/docs/workflows/index)**: Automate routine work, and connect Jira, ServiceNow and the other tools your team already uses.
- **[OneUptime AI](https://oneuptime.com/docs/ai/ai-sre)**: Investigates new incidents and alerts and posts a root cause analysis with citations. When you turn fixing on, it can open a pull request with a fix for your team to review.
- **[API, CLI and Terraform](https://oneuptime.com/docs/api-reference/api-reference)**: Automate OneUptime from your scripts and CI, and manage monitors, status pages and on-call as code.
- **[MCP server](https://oneuptime.com/docs/ai/mcp-server)** (`https://oneuptime.com/mcp`): Connect Claude, Cursor, VS Code with GitHub Copilot or any other client of the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and ask it to look into an incident, query logs and traces, acknowledge an alert or set up a monitor.

Step-by-step guides take one job from start to finish, on OneUptime Cloud or your own server: [Know When Your Website or API Is Down](https://oneuptime.com/docs/guides/website-down), [Get Paged by Phone, SMS or Push](https://oneuptime.com/docs/guides/paging) and [Publish a Status Page](https://oneuptime.com/docs/guides/status-page).

Everything else is in the [docs](https://oneuptime.com/docs/introduction/getting-started).

## Get started

### OneUptime Cloud

[Sign up](https://oneuptime.com/accounts/register) and create a project. The free plan needs no credit card.

### Self-host with Docker Compose

You need a Linux server with at least 8 GB of memory. On a new Ubuntu, Debian or RHEL-based server, one command installs Docker, Git and Node.js where they are missing, asks for the address people will use and starts OneUptime:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://oneuptime.com/install.sh | bash
```

Or do it step by step, with Docker, Docker Compose, Git and Node.js installed. In step 3, put the domain name or IP address people will use to reach OneUptime in place of `<your-address>`, without `http://`: that is `HOST` in `config.env`. Keep `localhost` only to try OneUptime on your own computer.

```bash
# 1. Clone the release branch
git clone --depth 1 --single-branch --branch release https://github.com/OneUptime/oneuptime.git
cd oneuptime

# 2. Create your config
cp config.example.env config.env

# 3. Set HOST to the address people will use
sed -i.bak "s/^HOST=.*/HOST=<your-address>/" config.env && rm config.env.bak

# 4. Start everything
npm start
```

`npm start` checks the server, gives every secret in `config.env` its own random value and starts OneUptime. When it prints **OneUptime is up!**, open `http://localhost`, or your server's address, and sign up. The first account becomes the instance's admin.

Then follow the [Self-Hosting Guide](https://oneuptime.com/docs/installation/self-hosting-guide) through HTTPS, email and SMS to your first page. The [Docker Compose guide](https://oneuptime.com/docs/installation/docker-compose) covers server sizes, backups and updates.

### Kubernetes with Helm

For production at scale, or high availability, install the Helm chart. Set `host` to the domain name or IP address people will use to reach OneUptime:

```bash
helm repo add oneuptime https://helm-chart.oneuptime.com/
helm install my-oneuptime oneuptime/oneuptime --set host=oneuptime.example.com
```

The [chart's README](/HelmChart/Public/oneuptime/README.md) covers storage, HTTPS, databases and upgrades.

## Community and Enterprise

- **Community Edition**: Free and open source, with everything above, including SAML and OIDC single sign-on.
- **Enterprise Edition**: Adds SCIM provisioning, audit logs, team compliance and instance health dashboards, with priority support. Production use needs a license: [contact sales](mailto:sales@oneuptime.com).

The docs [compare the two editions](https://oneuptime.com/docs/self-hosted/enterprise).

## Get help

- Ask questions in the [OneUptime community on Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/oneuptimesupport/shared_invite/zt-2pz5p1uhe-Fpmc7bv5ZE5xRMe7qJnwmA).
- Report bugs and request features in [GitHub issues](https://github.com/OneUptime/oneuptime/issues).
- Report a security vulnerability privately, as [SECURITY.md](/.github/SECURITY.md) explains.
- Email [support@oneuptime.com](mailto:support@one

readme.markdown:
# Infrahub MCP Server

Infrahub MCP Server connects AI assistants and IDE agents to [Infrahub](https://github.com/opsmill/infrahub) using the open [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) standard — so agents can query, create, update, and propose changes to your infrastructure data through a consistent, audited interface. It works with any MCP-compatible client (Claude Desktop, VS Code, Cursor, CLI agents, and more) with no custom glue code required.

All writes are branch-isolated and require human approval before merging — agents never modify your default branch directly.

## Installation

```bash
pip install infrahub-mcp
# or
uv pip install infrahub-mcp
```

Docker:

```bash
docker pull registry.opsmill.io/opsmill/infrahub-mcp:latest
# or use Docker Compose:
docker compose up -d
```

## Quickstart

Point the server at your Infrahub instance via environment variables, then run it over the transport your client expects.

**stdio** (default — for Claude Desktop, VS Code, Cursor):

```bash
export INFRAHUB_ADDRESS=http://localhost:8000
export INFRAHUB_API_TOKEN=<your-token>
infrahub-mcp
```

**Streamable HTTP** (for remote clients, sidecar deployments):

```bash
infrahub-mcp --transport streamable-http --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8001
```

## What you can do with it

- **Query your infrastructure data from natural language** — find devices, interfaces, IP addresses, or any kind in your schema, with attribute filtering and partial-match search.
- **Explore your schema without leaving the conversation** — the server exposes your catalog, per-kind attribute/filter maps, and the GraphQL SDL as MCP resources.
- **Make changes on isolated branches** — writes land on an auto-created session branch (`mcp/session-YYYYMMDD-<hex>`); the default branch is never touched directly.
- **Submit changes for human review** — call `propose_changes` to open a Proposed Change for approval before merging.
- **Run arbitrary GraphQL** — execute any query or mutation against the Infrahub API when you need full control.

## Documentation

Full documentation, including client configuration for Cursor, VS Code, Claude Desktop, and Claude Code, is available at the [Infrahub MCP Server docs site](https://docs.infrahub.app/mcp).

- [Installation and client setup](https://docs.infrahub.app/mcp/getting-started/installation)
- [Docker / sidecar deployment](https://docs.infrahub.app/mcp/guides/docker-compose)
- [Authentication modes](https://docs.infrahub.app/mcp/references/authentication)
- [Configuration reference](https://docs.infrahub.app/mcp/references/configuration)
- [Methods reference — tools, resources, prompts](https://docs.infrahub.app/mcp/references/methods)

## About Infrahub

[Infrahub](https://github.com/opsmill/infrahub) is an open source infrastructure data management and automation platform (AGPLv3), developed by [OpsMill](https://opsmill.com). It gives infrastructure and network teams a unified, schema-driven source of truth — devices, topology, IP space, configuration — with built-in version control, a generator framework for automation, and native integrations with Git, Ansible, Terraform, and CI/CD pipelines.

readme.markdown: Orangescrum MCP Server The official Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for Orangescrum: a cloud-hosted bridge that gives your AI tools secure, real-time access to projects, tasks, users, sprints, Test Case Management, releases, Scaled Agile, risk, resource, attendance, and leave management, the Knowledge Base (Wiki), and documents in your Orangescrum workspace. Getting started · Supported tools · Security & admin · Troubleshooting --- The **official Orangescrum MCP Server** is a cloud-based bridge between your Orangescrum workspace and compatible AI tools. Once connected, it lets those tools work with **projects, tasks, users, the epic, feature, and story hierarchy, sprints, timelogs, Test Case Management, versions and releases, Scaled Agile, risk management, resource management, attendance, leave, checklists, Knowledge Base (Wiki) pages, saved project context, and uploaded documents** in real time. Authentication uses **OAuth 2.1 with PKCE**, so every action runs as the signed-in user and respects their existing Orangescrum roles and permissions. With the Orangescrum MCP Server, you can: * **Summarize and search** projects, tasks, sprints, defects, releases, Wiki pages, and documents without switching tools. * **Create and update** tasks, stories, defects, test cases, timelogs, releases, and Knowledge Base pages from natural language. * **Plan and track** sprints, program increments, and release readiness with live data. * **Automate repetitive work**, like turning meeting notes into tasks or a spec into a backlog. Connect once, then describe what you want. There is no tab switching and no copy-pasting: your AI selects and runs the right actions. It's built for project managers, developers, QA teams, and delivery leads who work in AI assistants or IDEs and want to use Orangescrum data without constantly switching context. > [!IMPORTANT] > **The recommended endpoint is `https://mcp.orangescrum.com/mcp/partner`.** It uses OAuth 2.1, so you never paste an API key into a config file. Your client registers itself, opens a browser for you to sign in, and asks you to pick one workspace. For setup steps, see [Quickstart](https://helpdesk.orangescrum.com/guide/mcp/quickstart). ## One-click setup Pick your AI client below to add the official Orangescrum MCP Server. **One-click install** buttons add the server for you, so you don't need to edit any JSON config by hand. The others open that client's step-by-step guide. Claude Custom connector Claude Code One command Codex One command ChatGPT Custom connector VS Code One-click install OpenCode One command Gemini Custom app Antigravity IDE and CLI Perplexity Custom connector Cursor One-click install Muse Chat prompt Hermes Agent config.yaml OpenClaw One command GitHub Copilot CLI and IDE Grok Custom connector Kiro One-click install Devin Desktop Settings Zed Settings LM Studio mcp.json n8n Workflow node More than 70 clients are covered in the client guides. ### Let your agent do the setup Most AI agents can add the server and start the sign-in themselves. Read https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Orangescrum/orangescrum-mcp-server/main/INSTALL.md and follow it exactly: add the server https://mcp.orangescrum.com/mcp/partner using my client's own method, keep my existing MCP servers, walk me through the browser sign-in, then call get_current_user to confirm it works. ``` [INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md) tells the agent how to find its own client's steps, add the server without touching other settings, hand the sign-in to you, and check the connection. Or add the server yourself: | Client | Command or configuration | | --- | --- | | Claude Code | `claude mcp add --transport http orangescrum https://mcp.orangescrum.com/mcp/partner`, then `/mcp` to sign in | | Codex CLI | `codex mcp add orangescrum --url https://mcp.orangescrum.com/mcp/partner`, then `codex mcp login orangescrum` | | OpenCode | Add `{"mcp": {"orangescrum": {"type": "remote", "url": "https://mcp.orangescrum.com/mcp/partner"}}}` to `opencode.json`, then `opencode mcp auth orangescrum` | | GitHub Copilot CLI | `copilot mcp add --transport http orangescrum https://mcp.orangescrum.com/mcp/partner`, then `/mcp auth` | | Cursor | Add `{"mcpServers": {"orangescrum": {"url": "https://mcp.orangescrum.com/mcp/partner"}}}` to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | | VS Code | Add `{"servers": {"orangescrum": {"type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.orangescrum.com/mcp/partner"}}}` to `.vscode/mcp.json` | | Google Antigravity | Add `{"mcpServers": {"orangescrum": {"serverUrl": "https://mcp.orangescrum.com/mcp/partner"}}}` to `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json` | | Claude.ai / Claude Desktop | **Customize → Connectors → + Add → Add custom connector**, name it `Orangescrum`, and paste the server URL | | ChatGPT | **chatgpt.com/plugins → + → Add custom MCP server**, paste the server URL, and cho …

readme.markdown:
# PlaywrightGen

Playwright tests written from your real page, run until they pass, and kept as
evidence a person approved.

Live at [playwrightgen.com](https://playwrightgen.com).

Writing a Playwright test is no longer the hard part — every editor has an
assistant that will do it. What none of them keep is the thing an audit, a
release decision or a customer actually asks for: which behaviour was agreed,
by whom, at which version, and what the last run proved. That record is what
this product is.

## How it works

Two ways in, one chain.

**The free tools** need no account. Say what to test, paste a public URL, and
PlaywrightGen reads the page, writes a test from its real accessibility tree,
runs it in a remote browser, and fixes the failing step until it passes. You
get working code and the run that proves it, signed so the evidence survives
if you later bring it into a workspace. Nothing durable is claimed until you
do.

**The workspace** turns that into a record:

1. A **Requirement** is drafted, reviewed and approved. Approving writes an
   immutable version.
2. **Test Cases** carry objective, steps and expected results, are approved
   the same way, and link to the Requirements they verify.
3. **Automation** is generated from an approved Test Case version, validated
   against deterministic rules, proven on the live page, and then approved by
   a person — never by the generator and never by an agent.
4. **Run evidence** arrives from your own CI. Your tests run on your runners,
   against your environment, with your secrets; only a bounded summary of
   results is sent. A `[pwg:...]` marker in the test title is what ties a
   result to the approved version it is evidence for.
5. **A proof link** shares the result outside the team: a signed URL anybody
   can open, with an acceptance signature and a downloadable file they can
   keep.

Every claim on that chain names its source. A requirement with no passing test
says so; a run that was skipped says it proved nothing; a report that was
bounded says how much it did not cover.

## What holds it honest

- **A prompt is a request; a validator is a rule.** Every promise a prompt
  makes has a deterministic check behind it: no focused tests, no fixed
  sleeps, no credentials in the file, no request to an address that is not the
  application under test, no Node capability a browser test has no business
  reaching for.
- **A repair may not weaken a test.** The quickest way to make a failing
  assertion pass is to delete it, so a fix that checks less than the test it
  was given is refused.
- **Separation of duties.** The person who proposed something cannot be the
  one who approves it; the MCP server can propose and send code and has no
  capability to approve, accept, share or delete, which a test enforces by
  reading the import graph.
- **Every AI surface is measured.** `npm run evals` grades each prompt
  deterministically against structured output and compares the run with a
  hand-blessed baseline.

## For agents (MCP)

PlaywrightGen is an MCP server, so Claude Code, Cursor or Copilot can read the
approved intent instead of guessing: sixteen tools covering requirements, test
cases, approved automation, recent failures, writing and proving a test on a
live page, and proposing drafts for review. An agent gets exactly the rights
of the person whose token it used.

## Running it locally

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Then `npm run test:run` for the suite, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint`,
and `npm run build`. Integration tests need `TEST_DATABASE_URL` pointing at a
database used for nothing else; they refuse anything that looks like
production.

Built with Next.js, TypeScript, PostgreSQL (Prisma), Clerk, Tailwind,
Playwright, OpenAI and Stripe.

## Environment

Runtime:

- `DATABASE_URL` — PostgreSQL for the application.
- `DIRECT_URL` — optional direct connection preferred by migration commands.
- `TEST_DATABASE_URL` — a separate database for integration tests. It never
  falls back to either of the above.
- `NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY`, `CLERK_SECRET_KEY`,
  `CLERK_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET`
- `OPENAI_API_KEY` — server-only. Per-surface model overrides exist, for
  example `OPENAI_REQUIREMENT_REVIEW_MODEL` and
  `OPENAI_FAILURE_ANALYSIS_MODEL`.
- `UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL`, `UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_TOKEN` — the per-minute and
  per-day AI allowances.
- `RUNNER_INGEST_SECRET` — signs live-run receipts, so a receipt proves a run
  of that exact code.
- `BROWSERLESS_API_KEY` — the remote browser the free tools and proving use.
- `EXAMPLE_EVIDENCE_PROJECT_ID` — optional: the one project whose evidence is
  published publicly at `/proof/example`.

GitHub integration (separate values per environment):

- `GITHUB_APP_ID`, `GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY`, `GITHUB_APP_SLUG`,
  `GITHUB_APP_CLIENT_ID`, `GITHUB_APP_CLIENT_SECRET`, `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`
- `GITHUB_SETUP_STATE_SECRET` — at least 32 characters, distinct from every
  other secret.
- `NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL` — the exact origin the GitHub callback returns to.

The App is held to a permission ceiling, checked on every installation and
refused if exceeded: `metadata: read`, `contents: read` and `write`,
`pull_requests: read` and `write`, `issues: read`. Contents write is what
opens a pull request with approved test code; pull-requests write is what
leaves the evidence note on it; issues read is what drafts a requirement from
a ticket. User and installation tokens are transient and are never logged or
stored.

Clerk webhooks go to `/api/webhooks/clerk` with
`CLERK_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET` set locally and in the deployment, subscribed
to:

- `user.created`, `user.updated`, `user.deleted`
- `organization.created`, `organization.updated`, `organization.deleted`
- `organizationMembership.created`, `organizationMembership.updated`,
  `organizationMembership.deleted`

Local webhook delivery needs a secure tunnel to the local application. Never
put a webhook secret in documentation or source contr
